The national forests, comprising over 181,- 000,000 acres, are located in 39 States and Puerto Rico. The Forest Service improves them, protects them from fire, insects, and disease, and manages their resources for orderly and continuous service and for the maintenance of stable economic conditions in national forest communities. National forests are managed under the twin conservation policies of multiple use and sustained yield. Technical methods of forestry are applied to the growing and harvesting of timber. 

Livestock grazing is scientifically regu lated to obtain range conservation along with use of the annual growth of forage. Watersheds are managed for the regulation of streamflow, reduction of flood danger and soil erosion, and the protection of sources of water for power, irrigation, navigation, and municipal and domestic supply. Provision is made for popular outdoor recreation. Scientific management is applied to the development and maintenance of wildlife resources. 

In 1960 Congress gave legislative confirmation to these guiding principles by passage of the Multiple Use Sustained Yield Act, which directs that the national forests be developed and administered for their several basic products and services, i.e., outdoor recreation, range, timber, watershed, and wildlife and fish. It authorizes the Secretary of Agriculture to cooperate with States, local government agencies, and others. This new law, along with the 1897 act outlining a system of organization and manage-

ment for these public forests, provides the fundamental charter for nationalforest management and development. 

FOREST RESEARCH. In 10 regional forest and range experiment stations, in the Institute of Tropical Forestry in Puerto Rico, and in the Forest Products Laboratory at Madison, Wis., and a research unit in Hawaii, the Forest 

Service conducts investigations in the entire field of forestry and wild land management, including the growth and harvesting of timber, protection of forests from fire, insects, and diseases, management of range lands, efficient and economical utilization of forest products, and research in forest economics and taxation and watershed management. It is conducting a forest survey of the United States. This is a study of the Nation's present and potential forest resources.

COOPERATION IN FORESTRY.-States and private owners of forest lands and forest industries receive cooperation from the Forest Service. Assistance is provided in the application of sound forest management practices, in the maintenance of organized protection of forest lands against fire, in forest pest control, in flood prevention and river basin programs, and in the distribution of trees for planting woodlands, windbreaks, and shelterbelts.

The Service cooperates with States to stimulate development, proper administration, and management of State and community forests. It also ad ministers the Naval Stores Conser vation Program and assists in the administration of the forestry practices involved in the agricultural conservation program. 

Rural Electrification Administration 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 6, Chapter II] The Rural Electrification Adminis tration was created by Executive 

Order 7037 of May 11, 1935, under authority of the Emergency Relief 220 

Appropriation Act of 1935, approved 

April 8, 1935 (49 Stat. 115). Statutory provision for the agency was made in the Rural Electrification Act of May 

20, 1936 (49 Stat. 1363; 7 U. S. C. 

901 et seq.). This law authorizes loans for facilities to bring initial and continued adequate central station elec tric service to persons in rural areas who do not have it. REA became a part of the Department of Agriculture under Reorganization Plan II, effective July 1, 1939. An act approved Septem ber 21, 1944 (58 Stat. 739; 7 U.S.C. 

903), liberalized the terms of REA loans and removed the time limitation from its lending program. REA is authorized by act approved October 

28, 1949 (63 Stat. 948; 7 U.S.C. 901), th to make loans for the purpose of furnishing and improving rural telephone service. 

LOAN TERMS.-The act of Septem ber 21, 1944, established the interest rate on all REA loans at 2 percent, and fixed the permissible loan period at a maximum of 35 years.

APPLICATIONS FOR LOANS.-Upon inquiry, REA will furnish full information on the methods of applying for rural electric and telephone system loans. If an application is approved by the Administrator after legal, engineering, economic, and financial studies, funds are obligated by a loan contract and the borrower gives a note, mortgage, and in some cases other security. Funds advanced as needed for carrying out the construction. are technical assistance in engineering, ac- 

REA furnishes its borrowers with counting, and operations in support of the security of the Government loans.

LOANS FOR RURAL ELECTRIC SERV- 

ICE.-The law provides that, in making electrification loans, preference shall be given to public bodies, cooperatives, and nonprofit or limited dividend associations. 

As of January 1, 1963, Congress had authorized electrification loan funds totaling $5,003,928,288 (cumulative),

271 and the agency had made loans in the amount of $4,786,351,219 to 1,096 borrowers for the construction of electric distribution, generation, and transmission facilities and for financing the purchase and installation of electrical appliances and equipment. Of this amount, $4,072,663,014 had been addvanced to the borrowers. 

Estimates indicate that these loans will enable the borrowers to construct 

1,540,473 miles of line and related 5 facilities to serve 5,620,189 farms and other rural establishments. Some of the loan funds will be used to increase the capacity of existing lines, made neces- Esary because of the increasing use of power by rural people, and for generation and transmission. As of September 30, 1962, 1,041 power systems, comprising about 1,496,000 miles of line, were in operation serving about 

5,067,000 consumers. 

Applications for electric loans totaling $217,149,000 were on file with

REA as of January 1, 1963. 

LOANS FOR WIRING, APPLIANCES, AND PLUMBING.-The Rural Electrification 

Act authorizes loans to finance the wiring of the premises of persons in rural areas and the acquisition and installation of electrical and plumbing appliances and equipment, including machinery. Such loans generally are required to be repaid within a period of 10 years. 

No loans are made direct to the consumer. The funds are loaned to REA borrowers operating electric systems for relending to their members.

LOANS FOR RURAL TELEPHONE SERV- 

ICE.-Loans are made to cooperatives and independent telephone companies for extending or improving service. A specific requirement of the rural telephone program, as set down by Congress, is that it be conducted so as to make telephone service available to the widest practicable number of rural users. Through fiscal year 1963, Congress had authorized $1,031,736,718 for telephone loans, and by January 1, 1963, REA had approved $930,421,- 

431 in loans to 797 borrowers to bring new or improved service to 1,782,185 subscribers in 46 States. As of the same date 723 telephone borrowers had 

3,180 new dial exchanges in operation.

Applications on hand in REA for telephone loans totaled $64,527,000 as of January 1, 1963. 

REPAYMENT OF LOANS.-By January 

1, 1963, electric borrowers had repaid $936,263,678 of principal and paid $558,120,623 in interest on their loans.

In addition, they had made payments ahead of schedule amounting to $203,- 

199,582. Only two electric borrowers were in arrears on payments for a total of $120,525.

In the newer telephone program, by the same date, the borrowers had repaid $42,785,797 of principal and $43,- 

968,249 in interest. Payments ahead of schedule amounted to $7,063,457. 

Six borrowers were overdue in payments amounting to $230,561. 

Soil Conservation Service 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 7, Chapter VI] The Soil Conservation Service was established under authority of the Soil 

Conservation Act of 1935 (49 Stat. 

163; 16 U.S.C. 590 a-f). It is the technical soil and water conservation agency of the Department of Agriculture, charged with the responsibility of developing and carrying out a permanent national soil and water conservation program. The SCS administers Department of Agriculture activities involving technical assistance in soil and water conservation and watershed protection and flood prevention on private land. It gives technical information and services needed by other agencies in related programs.

The work of the SCS is directed by the Administrator and his staff from the central office in Washington, D.C.

The SCS maintains 49 State offices and one Caribbean office which perform technical and administrative

functions to provide service to field personnel. Within the States, about 

285 area offices supervise about 3,000 work units where conservation technicians work directly with farmers and ranchers on the land. Technical specialists are located strategically throughout the United States to provide scientific and technical guidance and training to field personnel and to produce land-capability maps and other essential working materials. 

The primary job of the SCS is helping farmers and ranchers, individually or in groups, do conservation work on the land. The SCS provides this assistance mainly through locally organized, farmer-directed soil con servation districts. By January 1, 1963, there were 2,936 such districts in all 

50 States, Puerto Rico, and the Virgin 

Islands. They include 96 percent of the Nation's farms and 93 percent of its land in farms.

The assistance given to cooperators in districts involves four principal steps: 

First, a soil scientist makes a detailed, acre-by-acre soil survey of the farm or ranch. The SCS gives the operator a soil and land-capability map of his land. 

Second, the conservationist gives the farmer or rancher information about practical alternatives for treatment and use of the land within its capability, as indicated by the survey. 

Third, SCS technicians help the operator apply the parts of the plan that require special skills or knowledge. 

Fourth, the technicians give the guidance needed for maintaining and improving the farm or ranch conservation plan after it is applied to the land. 

To provide these services, the SCS brings together in one national staff the scientists and technicians needed to solve practical problems of land use and conservation. 

By July 1, 1962, technicians of the 

Service had helped 1,944,644 farmers and ranchers whose farms and ranches totaled 618,837,161 acres. Conservation plans had been prepared for 1,- 410,908 farms and ranches, including 

427,072,177 acres.

As an integral part of its national program, the SCS has leadership responsibility for the Federal part of the 

National Cooperative Soil Survey. The work is carried out in cooperation with the State agricultural experiment sta tions and other State and Federal agencies. Soil surveys provide basic soils information needed for soil and water conservation planning and for classification and development of nonagricultural lands. Survey reports are published by the Department. More than 740,000,000 acres had been surveyed and mapped by July 1, 1962, in enough detail for soil and water conservation planning of farms and ranches and small-watershed projects. The SCS has the responsibility for the watershed protection activities and the river basin surveys and investigations of the Department of Agriculture. 

Under authority of the Flood Con trol Act of 1944, the SCS plans and applies flood prevention measures and practices in 11 major watersheds comprising approximately 30 million acres. 

Detailed flood prevention plans are prepared and applied to tributary wa tersheds. The plans are used for scheduling quantities and types of measures to be applied or installed throughout the major watersheds, and for determining the relationships between flood prevention benefits and costs. 

In addition, the SCS is nearing completion of watershed protection planning and operations on 54 pilot watersheds provided for in the USDA Appropriation Act passed in 1953. The purpose of the program is to demonstrate the benefits of combining soil and water conservation on the land with upstream flood-prevention structures. Local organizations share the costs with the Federal Government.

The SCS has administrative leadership for Federal assistance to small-

watershed projects under the Water shed Protection and Flood Prevention Act (68 Stat. 666; 16 U.S.C. 10011007). The act, as amended, provides for technical and financial assistance by the Department of Agriculture to local organizations for land treatment, flood prevention, fish and wildlife development, recreation, and agricultural and municipal water supply on watersheds up to 250,000 acres in size. By March 1, 1963, 1,852 applications for assistance had been received. 

Of these, 841 had been authorized for planning assistance, of which 457 had been authorized for operations.

The SCS has administrative leadership of the Great Plains Conservation 

Program under the act of August 7, 1956 (70 Stat. 1115; 16 U.S.C. 590p).

The program is designed to help farmers and ranchers in designated counties in the Great Plains States initiate and complete conservation plans of operations over a 3-to-10-year period, through contracts that guarantee costsharing until the job is done. The plans are aimed at minimizing climatic hazards by helping farmers make land use adjustments and install soil and water conservation measures needed to achieve a more stable agriculture. 

By January 1, 1963, over 10,700 plans were in effect under the program. 

The SCS gives technical assistance in establishing income-producing recreation on private lands as a part of a conservation plan and is authorized to assist local sponsors in developing and carrying out resource conservation and development projects. 

The SCS provides on-site assistance in farm drainage and irrigation groups of farms, and makes and coordinates snow surveys for water forecasting in the Western States. It provides needed technical assistance to farmers and ranchers who participate in the agricultural conservation and cropland conversion programs of the 

Department of Agriculture. The SCS 

also gives technical help to the Farm ers Home Administration in making soil and water conservation loans to farmers and ranchers.

Agricultural Economics Economic Research Service The Economic Research Service 

(ERS) was created by Secretary's 

Memorandum 1446, Supplement 1, dated April 3, 1961, under authority of

Reorganization Plan 2 of 1953. 

The ERS conducts programs of research in agricultural economics and marketing, both domestic and in foreign commerce. Marketing economics research is authorized under the Research and Marketing Act of 1946.

Farm economics research work traces back to early farm management work and has been conducted in various organization units since 1905. Program activities are described in the following paragraphs.

ECONOMIC AND STATISTICAL ANAL- 

YSIS.-Agricultural economics research includes broad economic and analysis programs on factors affecting agricultural prices and income, commodity outlook and situation, food demand, consumption, and supply. The relationships between the farm economy and the national economy are studied, as are the economic forces affecting general levels of demand, prices, and incomes in agriculture. 

An important program of research is concerned with population, farm manpower, levels of living, rural development and problems. This research provides useful information on the economic status of farmers, the relation of farm income to nonfarm income, and the outlook for agriculture generally. Farmers and others are provided with essential information to help them adjust to economic forces affecting prices, supply, and consump-

tion of agricultural products and to understand conditions affecting farm people or the agricultural economy.

MARKETING ECONOMICS RESEARCH.- 

Marketing research is concerned with market costs, structure, and development, market potentials, and the distribution and merchandising of agricultural products. Studies are conducted to determine the potentials for market expansion of agricultural products. 

The movement of agricultural products through marketing channels and the economic aspects of public distribution programs are studied to obtain information to aid agricultural industries in improving the merchandising of their products. Cost analysis research is conducted on the marketing of crops and animal products to determine ways of increasing efficiency and reducing costs, increasing returns to growers and providing consumers with the choices they desire. Emphasis in marketing research is placed on products in abundant supply requiring additional outlets. The research results are widely disseminated. 

FARM PRODUCTION ECONOMICS RE- 

SEARCH.-ERS administers a national program of economic and statistical research on farm problems involving the efficient use of labor, land, buildings, and equipment in farm production, and adjustment in farming to technological development and changing market outlets. Research on farming efficiency includes studies of farm labor, trends in mechanization and other technological developments, electrification, farm structures, fertilizer and pesticide usage, and livestock feeding practices. Research on production, income, and costs involves appraisals of farm output and productivity (nationally and by commodity and region), studies of costs and returns on important types of farms, and problems of low-production farms and their opportunities for income improvement. Studies of agricultural finance deal with farm credit facilities, financing of farm-living and production, agricultural risk and insurance problems, accident statistics, farm real estate values, and impact of taxation upon individual farmers and agriculture as an industry.

RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT ECONOMICS RESEARCH. National programs of economic research, technical consultation, and service work are conducted on the extent, use, development, and management of natural resources. 

Land and water research involves studies of economic utilization of land and water resources, the impact of urban and industrial expansion, land tenure problems, legal-economic aspects of land and water use, and the relationship of resource utilization and tenure to income and values. River basin and watershed investigations are conducted relating to the formulation. of comprehensive river basin plans and programs, watershed planning, development and management programs, and resource conservation projects. 

Area economic development research includes analyses of the characteristics, income, and employment opportunities of chronic rural depressed areas, and problems of rural renewal and economic development or growth.

FOREIGN REGIONAL ANALYSIS.-ERS 

makes economic analyses and interpretations of conditions and development affecting supply, demand, and trade in farm products in foreign countries and their impact on U.S. agricultural exports. The work includes research on the total food and agricultural situation by countries and regions. Annual food budgets are prepared as well as key indices reflecting changes in agricultural production by countries, regions, and for the world. Studies are conducted on the long-range outlook for U.S. agricultural exports, based in part on research contracts with foreign institutions to project the demand and supply of farm products in foreign countries for several years ahead.

Trends in supply and demand throughout the world are analyzed together with their implications for resource

adjustment and agricultural policy in the United States.

DEVELOPMENT AND TRADE ANALY- 

SIS.-Economic development processes in foreign countries are analyzed to ascertain the contribution of agricultural development to general economic growth, the priority of various aspects of agricultural development, trends in national income, and economic effects of present and proposed 

Food for Peace programs. Analysis of the effects of Food for Peace and other U.S. farm export programs on trade and economic growth in foreign countries is carried out in part through research contracts with foreign institutions. The effects of alternative U.S. export programs and policies on domestic farm income and foreign trade are analyzed. Studies are made of monetary and financial problems of foreign countries and their effects on U.S. exports of farm products. Agricultural policies and programs of foreign countries are studied, including the effects on U.S. exports of price support and production control programs, import fees and quotas, trade agreements and concessions, and customs unions. Monthly, annual, and special agricultural trade statistics are developed and published. 

Statistical Reporting Service 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 7, Chapter XII] The Statistical Reporting Service, created by Secretary's Memorandum 

1446, Supplement 1, dated April 3, 1961, administers (1) a program concerned with the review, coordination, and improvement of statistics in the 

Department, and (2) crop and livestock estimates and reporting programs. 

STATISTICAL STANDARDS.-The Serv ice seeks to improve statistical methods and techniques throughout the Department through counseling, investigation of alternative methods and techniques, and the development of new techniques. The Service analyzes proposed plans for the collection of statistical data for use in the research, service, regulatory, and other programs of the Department to insure (a) that proposed plans and forms meet acceptable standards; (b) that forms for collecting data are well designed; and (c) that proposed plans do not duplicate data available from other sources. 

SRS operates the Washington, D.C., Data Processing Center of the Department. It carries out functions of systems analysis, programing, and processing of data by electronic and electromechanical equipment. SRS provides technical consulting services on statistical methods and techniques to other USDA agencies and represents the Department at meetings with other Federal agencies concerning statistical survey plans, report forms, and recordkeeping requirements. 

CROP AND LIVESTOCK ESTIMATES. 

The SRS prepares estimates and reports of production, supply, price, and other aspects of the agricultural economy. These include prices received by farmers for products sold and prices paid by farmers for commodities and services; preparation of indexes of prices received and paid; and computation of parity prices, farm employment, and wage rates. 

The reports include statistics on field crops, fruits and vegetables, and numbers of milk cows, livestock, livestock products, and poultry. The Service also carries out enumerative and objective measurement surveys and provides technical consultation and support for U.S. technicians overseas. 

Data upon which the crop and livestock estimates are based are collected, summarized, and evaluated in 43 field offices operated in cooperation with 

State agencies under the direction of an SRS statistician. The field offices cover all 50 States. The State and national offices prepare monthly, annual, and other periodic reports for distribution to news media and to the general public.

Departmental Administration Office of Budget and Finance The Office of Budget and Finance provides policy direction, review, and coordination of all budgetary and financial activities of the Department. 

This includes the acquisition and distribution of funds; accounting; budgetary and program analysis and appraisal; budgetary, financial, and legislative reporting; fiscal management; and the development and issuance of related policies and regulations. The 

Office represents the Department in contacts with the Budget Bureau, Gen eral Accounting Office, Treasury De partment, congressional committees on appropriations, and others concerned with these activities.

Office of Hearing Examiners The Office of Hearing Examiners was established by Secretary's Memorandum 1180, of December 9, 1946, to conform to the requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act, approved June 11, 1946 (60 Stat. 237; 

5 U. S. C. 1001-11). The Hearing 

Examiners hold hearings and perform related duties (1) required by sections 7 and 8 of that act, including proceedings arising under the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act of 

1937 (7 U. S. C. 601 et seq.), ratemaking and disciplinary proceedings under the Packers and Stockyards Act (7 U. S. C. 181 et seq.), and disciplinary proceedings under the Commodity Exchange Act (7 U. S. C. 1 et seq.), the Perishable Agricultural Commodities Act (7 U. S. C. 499a et seq.), the

Federal Seed Act (7 U. S. C. 1551 et seq.), and the Grain Standards Act (7 U. S. C. 71 et seq.); and (2) pursuant to departmental regulations governing other regulatory and service activities. 

Office of Information 

The Office of Information provides policy direction, review, and coordination of all information programs of the Department. This includes the final review, illustrating, printing, and distribution of publications; clearance and release of press, radio, television, and magazine materials; maintenance of central files of news and general illustration-type photographs; and the preparation and distribution of exhibits and motion pictures. The Office also produces visual information materials, such as motion pictures, exhibits, art and graphics materials, and still photographic work for the Department and other Government agencies.

Office of Management Appraisal and Systems Development 

The Office of Management Appraisal and Systems Development was established on December 8, 1961, to provide leadership to the Department's management improvement program.

The Office is responsible for the general direction, coordination, and technical guidance of: managmeent appraisals, operations research activities, systems engineering, and the acquisition and utilization of data processing equipment.

National Agricultural Library The National Agricultural Library provides services to agricultural colleges and universities, research institutions, Government agencies, agricul tural associations, industry, individual scientists, farmers, and the general public. 

With resources of almost 1,200,000 volumes, next to the Library of Congress it is the largest U.S. Government library in existence. It is the largest agricultural library in the United

States, covering the field of agriculture in the broadest sense-botany, zoology, chemistry, veterinary medicine, forestry, plant estry, plant pathology, livestock, poultry, entomology, and general agri-

WDW/ 

277 nd and ppr culture. Publications are received received reg- ularly from more than 200 countries, printed in approximately 50 different languages. 

Information contained in the Library's collection is disseminated through loans, photocopies, reference services, and bibliographies, including the Bibliography of Agriculture, a comprehensive listing of substantive agricultural books, reports, pamphlets, and articles.

These services and information from the collection are available to anyone, both in the United States and abroad. 

Office of Personnel The Office of Personnel provides her general direction, leadership, and coordination of the personnel management program of the Department. 

This includes organization, classification and standards, salary and wage administration, examinations and employment, personnel and records security, standards of employee conduct, discipline, employee relations, appeals, employee development, health, safety and welfare, incentive awards, employee-management relations, legislation, personnel research, employee fringe benefits, intergroup programs, and other personnel activities.

Office of Plant and Operations The Office of Plant and Operations exercises general staff management direction of the housing of the Department's activities, including real property, procurement, supply and property operations, Department motor vehicle fleet program, and records and paperwork programs. In addition it provides certain centralized departmental services in the District of Columbia.

Office of Management Services The Office of Management Services was established on February 1, 1963, to provide centralized management support service to 17 offices and agencies of the Department. These services include budget, accounting, and related financial management; agency information; personnel, organization, and related services; and procurement, property, space, communications, messenger, paperwork management, and related services.

The following offices and agencies are serviced by the Office of Management Services: Office of the Secretary,

Office of Budget and Finance, Office of Hearing Examiners, Office of Manage ment Appraisal and Systems Development, Office of Personnel, Office of

Plant and Operations, Office of the Inspector General, Office of Rural Areas Development, Office of Information, National Agricultural Library, Office of the General Counsel, Farmer Cooperative Service, Commodity Ex change Authority, Cooperative State

Experiment Station Service, Economic Research Service, Statistical Reporting 

Service, and Staff Economists Group.

Office of the General Counsel The General Counsel is the chief law officer of the Department and the principal legal adviser of the Secretary.

He and his staff provide legal services for all programs, operations, and activities of the Department.

Office of the Inspector General 

The Inspector General is charged with the responsibility of rendering constructive audit and investigative service and related specialized professional assistance to the Office of the 

Secretary, agency heads, and all levels of management within the Department. 

All internal audit and investigative

Director activities in the Department were assigned to the Office of the Inspector 

General on December 21, 1962, in order to provide the Secretary and agency heads with an independent and objective review and appraisal service. Approved.

Department of Commerce was designated as such by the act of March 4, 1913 (37 Stat. 736; 5 U. S. C. 591), which reorganized the Department of 

Commerce and Labor, created by the act of February 14, 1903 (32 Stat. 825; 

5 U. S. C. 591), by transferring out of the former department all labor activities. 

PURPOSE.-The statutory functions of the Department are to foster, promote, and develop the foreign and domestic commerce, the manufacturing and shipping industries, and the transportation facilities of the United 

States. Related functions subsequently have been added to or eliminated from the Department from time to time by legislation or Executive order; however, the purposes have remained substantially the same as those for which the Department was established.

ORGANIZATION.-The Department of Commerce is composed of the Office of the Secretary and the offices and bureaus described below. The structure of the Department is shown in the organization chart which appears on page 600. 

ACTIVITIES.-The activities of the 

Department include population, agricultural, and other censuses; collection, analysis, and dissemination of commercial statistics; promotion of foreign and domestic commerce; coastal and geodetic surveys; compilation and publication of nautical and aeronautical charts; establishment of commodity weights, measures, and standards; issuance of patents and the registration of trademarks; supervision of the issuance of weather forecasts

States; the fostering and promoting of inland waterway transportation; the policing of the performance by the purchaser of the facilities of the 

Inland Waterways Corporation to assure the continuance of service substantially similar to that formerly provided by the Corporation in its operation; declassification and dissemination of scientific and technical data; administration of Federal funds for highway improvement; development and maintenance of an adequate and well-balanced American merchant marine; maintenance and operation of the Saint Lawrence Seaway in United

States territory; administering a system of mandatory pilotage on designated 

United States waters of the Great

Lakes; and determination of requirements for materials and commodities needed for defense, civilian, foreign, and other purposes.

 Regu lations, Title 13, Chapter III] ESTABLISHMENT AND MISSION.- The Area Redevelopment Adminis tration was established by the Secretary of Commerce by Department 

Order 171 of May 8, 1961, pursuant to authority vested in the Secretary of

Commerce by Reorganization Plan 5 

of 1950, and the Area Redevelopment 

Act (75 Stat. 47; 42 U.S.C. 2501). 

The Administration is responsible for effective administration of those phases of the Area Redevelopment Act that 享​版 ​RAVE ad

are the responsibility of the Department of Commerce. In addition, the 

Administration is responsible for assisting and advising the Secretary in executing the functions related to the 

Public Works Acceleration Act (76

ORGANIZATION.--The headquarters organization of the Area Redevelopment Administration comprises the Office of the Administrator, the Office of Administration and Finance, the

Office of Operations, the Office of Planning and Research, and the Office of Public Works Acceleration. In accordance with the terms of the Area

Redevelopment Act, a National Public 

Advisory Committee on Area Rede velopment serves to promote full exchange of views between the Government and the public, and an Area Redevelopment Advisory Policy Board (an interagency committee) helps assure coordinated action by Federal

Government agencies on area redevelopment matters. 

PROGRAMS.-With respect to areas designated by the Administrator as "redevelopment areas," the the govern- ing legislation authorizes certain Federal aids including: loans for industrial or commercial facilities and loans or grants for public facilities, technical assistance, and related information.

The Area Redevelopment Administra tion exercises program control and provides policy direction for these activities with the assistance and cooperation of other Federal agencies.

With respect to the Public Works Acceleration Act, the Administrator, in order to increase employment opportunities, prepares for the Secretary recommendations as to the public works to be initiated and/or accelerated in those areas designated as eligible by the Secretary of Labor or designated as redevelopment areas by the Administrator. 

The Secretary of Commerce has delegated operating functions under the Area Redevelopment Act to the 

Departments of Agriculture, Health, Education, and Welfare, Interior, and Labor, and to the Housing and

Home Finance Agency and the Small 

Business Administration. These functions include technical assistance and economic development information as well as the processing of loan and grant applications. In addition, the Administration utilizes a staff of field representatives to provide direct assistance to State and local agencies concerned with economic development.

Business and Defense Services Administration 

 Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter VI; Title 32A, Chapter VI; Title 44, Chapter IV]  Business and Defense Services Admin istration was established by the Secretary of Commerce by Department 

Order 152 of October 1, 1953, as a primary organization unit of the Department of Commerce, pursuant to authority vested in the Secretary of

Commerce by Reorganization Plan 5 

of 1950.

ORGANIZATION.-The Business and Defense Services Administration is headed by an Administrator who reports and is responsible to the 

Assistant Secretary for Domestic and

International Business. Program activities are executed by 24 industry divisions, grouped by related industries into the Offices of Distribution Services, Chemicals and Consumer Products, Industrial Equipment, Metals and Minerals, Scientific and Technical

Equipment, Construction and Materi als Industries, and Textiles. Program guidance is provided by Assistant Administrators in the functional areas of

Industrial Analysis, International Commodity Activities, Industrial Mo bilization, Business and Government 

Services, and Administration.

ACTIVITIES 

The agency carries on program activities designed to promote and develop the growth of industry and commerce of the United States, and performs national defense and industrial mobilization functions contributing to the national security.

BUSINESS AND GOVERNMENT SERV- 

ICES.-BDSA collects, analyzes, and disseminates industrial and commercial intelligence for the benefit of the business community and Government agencies, measures the impact on the domestic market of Government excess property disposals, and fosters a common understanding of the problems of Government and business and industry. 

INDUSTRIAL ANALYSIS.-The agen cy conducts economic research programs concerned with industrial growth and development of American business and industry, the impact of import competition on domestic industries, and the effects of factors such as technological change, automation, industrial research, and governmental fiscal and tax policies on the domestic economy. 

INTERNATIONAL COMMODITY ACTIVI- 

TIES.-The agency develops export potential for selected commodities, disseminates foreign trade opportunity information, analyzes the effect of international trade impediments on export trade, and furnishes commodity. industry information and technical advice in preparation for and in support of international trade negotiations and agreements. 

INDUSTRIAL MOBILIZATION.-BDSA 

administers the authority delegated to the Secretary of Commerce under the

Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended, with respect to the use of priorities and directives that are necessary to support and expedite the accomplishment of current military, atomic energy, and space programs; develops, under general guidance of the Office of Emergency Planning, plans for industrial mobilization and production control in an emergency; and provides advice and counsel to the 

Office of Emergency Planning on na tional stockpile operations.

Many of the services offered are available through the Department of Commerce field offices and through official cooperative offices of the Department.

Office of Business Economics 

 Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter VIII] The Office of Business Economics provides basic economic measures of the national economy, current analysis of the economic situation and business outlook, the United States balance of international payments, and general economic research on the functioning of the economy. For its analyses the 

Office develops economic and statistical indicators, and its national income and product work provides a basis for policy formulation by the Department, other executive agencies, and the Congress, with respect to Government operations insofar as they affect economic movements. Its services to business are long established and well known through the official monthly journal 

Survey of Current Business. The Office of Business Economics organi zation includes five major operating units: National Income Division, Current Business Analysis Division, Business Structure Division, National Economics Division, and the Balance of Payments Division.

Bureau of the Census  Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter I] 

The Bureau of the Census is a factfinding and statistical service agency for the Federal Government. Through its basic program, benchmark and current statistics are furnished to Government, to business, to research groups, and to individuals. Census taking was established by the Constitution for the primary purpose of determining the population basis for apportioning Representatives and direct taxes among the States. A population census has been taken decennially, beginning in 

1790, and since 1810 other subjects have regularly been included. Prior to 

1902, each census was taken by an ad hoc organization, but in 1902 the Cen- Onsus Bureau was established and has functioned since then as a permanent agency for taking censuses and carrying out general-purpose statistical projects as assigned.

PE The schedule of major censuses regularly taken by the Bureau is now as follows: population, every 10 years, taken in years ending in 0; housing, every 10 years, taken in years ending in 

0; agriculture, every 5 years, taken in years ending in 4 and 9; manufactures, mineral industries, business (retail trade, wholesale trade, and selected services), and transportation, every 5 years, covering years ending in 3 and 8 (the first census of transportation is being conducted for 1963); governmental units, every 5 years, covering years ending in 2 and 7. 

Every 10 years, in years ending in 9, census of drainage and a census of irrigation are taken, augmenting the census of agriculture. The collection of current data at monthly, quarterly, or annual intervals provides up-to-date information on many of the subjects covered in the major censuses, on construction activity, and on the foreign trade of the 

United States. Additional inquiries are inaugurated, as required, to meet new problems faced by Government agencies, and by business, industry, and research interests.

The results of the major censuses provide comprehensive national statistics and information in considerable subject detail. These censuses also furnish facts on an area basis not possible with sample surveys conducted between census years. Each census provides area data for States and counties; in addition, figures for other areas are available as follows: the business census provides statistics for standard metropolitan statistical areas (SMSA's), urban places, and the central business district of large cities; the manufactures census provides data for 

SMSA's and urban places; minerals, for counties making up SMSA's; and the population and housing censuses provide data for small areas, including statistics on population and housing for census tracts and on housing for city blocks. The census of governments provides information for 

SMSA's, townships, municipalities, school districts, and special districts.

The 1963 census of transportation will provide some statistics for States.

STATISTICAL SERVICES ΤΟ OTHER AGENCIES.-The Bureau collects and tabulates data for other agencies in addition to the statistical material provided in the course of its regular work; and the technical staff of the Bureau acts in an advisory capacity for other

Government agencies, assisting them in the full use of Census data and facilities. The Bureau provides, on a reimbursable basis, services in the solution of technical problems and for handling overflow jobs more efficiently than could be achieved by the creation of temporary staffs. These activities fall most frequently in the fields of sample design for surveys, collection of data, and machine tabulation. The latter service includes not only pro-

cedural and program planning, card punching, and tabulation, but developmental assistance in design and al teration of tabulating equipment. The 

Bureau's high-speed electronic equipment contributes to the efficient processing of mass statistical data and may be utilized in such projects for other agencies. The extensive collection of maps greatly facilitates survey design, data collection, and identification of material by geographic units. 

The services for handling statistical materials and for conducting impartial fact-finding surveys are available on a cost basis to any Federal agency. 

The Bureau is prepared to provide statistical services for defense mobilization agencies. These services in the past have ranged from acting as collecting and compiling agents for new surveys required by the defense effort, to special tabulations and analyses of already collected data in the areas of manufactures, business, population, foreign trade, and other subjects.

POPULATION.-The number, loca tion, and personal and family characteristics of the population, such as age, sex, race, marital status, place of birth, mother tongue of the foreign born, work status, occupation, education, migration, and income, are included in the decennial census of population. 

The current population survey, based on a scientifically selected sample of the population, is conducted monthly. At intervals this survey provides estimates of personal and family characteristics of the population, internal migration, school enrollment, educational attainment, number and characteristics of households, income, and consumer buying intentions. Responsibility for the publication and analysis of monthly statistics on the labor force, the employed, the unemployed, and their characteristics, based on the current population survey, was transferred, effective July 1, 1959, from the Department of Commerce to the Department of Labor. The Bureau of the Census continues to collect and tabulate the data as an agent of the 

Bureau of Labor Statistics. 

Estimates of the total population are prepared and published monthly; annual estimates for the country as a whole by age, sex, and color, and annual estimates by States are also published. Population projections for the 

United States by age, sex, and color are also issued from time to time. Special censuses of local areas are taken at the request and expense of the governments of these areas. 

HOUSING. Statistics on the number and characteristics of housing units are provided by the decennial census of housing. These include statistics on such characteristics as number of rooms, bedrooms, year built, tenure, value or rent, vacancy status, persons per room, water supply, toilet and bathing facilities, and equipment (including clothes washing machines, clothes dryers, radios, television sets, and the like).

As part of the 1960 decennial census, information was collected on components of inventory change and residential finance for the United States and 17 selected SMSA's. The components-of-inventory-change portion measures gains and losses in the housing inventory through new construction, conversion, demolition, and the like. The residential finance portion provides data on such mortgage char acteristics as amount of loan, interest rate, Government insurance status, method and amount of mortgage payments, and type of lender. 

Current statistics on housing include quarterly data on vacancy rates and condition and characteristics of available housing vacancies for the country as a whole, for geographic regions, and whether metropolitan or nonmetropolitan. Data on ownership of television sets for the Nation, regions, and geographic divisions have been obtained from a series of sample surveys.

AGRICULTURE. The quinquennial census of agriculture provides infor-

alc O DO mation on the characteristics of farms and farm operators; farm income; acreage, production, and value of crops; value of horticultural specialties; and number of livestock and production of livestock products. The censuses of drainage and irrigation provide decennial information on the number and characteristics of irrigation and drainage enterprises, and the extent of irrigation and drainage of agricultural lands. 

Statistics on cotton ginnings by cotton ginnings by 

State and county are collected and published periodically during the cotton harvesting season and at the end of the ginning year. Detailed statistics on cotton production and distribution are published annually.

INDUSTRY.-Results of the quin quennial census of manufactures provide information on employment, payrolls, consumption of materials, shipments, value added by manufacture, inventories, and capital expenditures. The most recent census, covering the year 1958, includes more detailed data on consumption of materials than previously available. It also provides figures on the distribution of manufacturers sales, an item not covered since the 1939 census. New inquiries, covered in a 1957 survey as an adjunct to the census, relate to nonpayroll labor costs, assets and depreciation, maintenance and repair costs, and other costs such as rent, insurance, and taxes.

The current industrial statistics program of the Bureau includes an annual survey of manufactures conducted for intercensal years and about 80 series of monthly, quarterly, and annual "Current Industrial Reports" (formerly designated "Facts for Industry") on the current output, shipments, consumption, and stocks of the more important manufactured products. Also included is the monthly survey of sales, orders, and inventories undertaken jointly with the Office of Business

Economics. The annual survey of manufactures, conducted on a sample basis, provides key data for intercensal years for the period 1949-61. 

Results of the census of mineral industries provide key measures of activity in the mining of coal, iron, and other metals and minerals, and the extraction of oil and gas. These measures include employment, payrolls, value added in mining, and other subjects generally similar to those of the manufactures census.

BUSINESS. Results of the census of business cover retail trade, wholesale trade, selected services, amusements, hotels, tourist courts, and public merchandise warehouses. Area statistics are provided on number of establishments, total sales, employment, and payroll, by kind of business. Statistics are also provided on other subjects, such as employment size, legal form of organization, sales or receipts size, single units and multi-units, wholesale credit, and wholesale trade by commodity lines. 

National monthly estimates of the dollar volume sales, as well as end-ofmonth accounts receivable, of retail stores by kind of business are issued, with advance estimates in lesser detail issued 10 days after each report month. 

In addition to the national dollar volume estimates of sales, release of selected data for regions, divisions, and a few large States, and SMSA's was begun in 1963. A new release on the volume of service trades receipts also was begun in 1963. A new series showing weekly retail sales estimates was begun in May 1962. Estimates of yearend inventories held by retailers and regional distribution of sales are published by kind of business for the 

United States. Trends in wholesale trade sales and inventories, by kind of business, are issued monthly. Estimates of canned food stocks are issued seasonally. 

TRANSPORTATION.-The first census of transportation is being taken for 1963. Its primary purpose is to collect and publish data on major aspects of transportation for which statistics are

on not available from other government or private sources. To avoid unnecessary duplication, the census is being taken as a series of four projects, as follows: (1) National Travel Survey, that will be based on personal interview at a sample of households to collect information about out-of-town trips by all modes (including automobile) and to obtain selected information home-to-work transportation; (2)

Commodity Transportation Survey, that will measure traffic flows generated by manufacturing plants. The basic information will be obtained by sampling bills of lading or other shipping papers normally kept in traffic department files. The data will represent shipments by all modes of transportation, including private trucking; (3) Truck Inventory and Use Survey, that will collect a wide range of facts concerning the number of trucks and combinations, such as (a) physical characteristics of vehicles, (b) major occupational use or type of service, and (c) rough indicators of the intensity of vehicle utilization; and (4) Bus and 

Truck Carrier Survey, that will obtain financial and operating data on "forhire" bus and truck carriers that are not federally regulated.

FOREIGN TRADE.-Reports are issued on the foreign trade of the United

States, including monthly and annual tabulations of information on imports and exports of merchandise and gold and silver, and statistics on trade of the continental United States with Puerto

Rico and with U.S. possessions. The tabulations contain detail as to commodities shipped, country of origin or destination, the trade through individual United States customs districts, etc. Information is also provided on export and import shipments by vessel and by air showing dollar value and shipping weight, and commodity totals of vessel shipments by port of lading and unlading and flag of vessel. Beginning with the October 1960 foreign trade statistics, figures are available on total exports (excluding military shipments) and total general imports adjusted for working day and seasonal variation. Figures on U.S. exports and imports by air are available on a monthly basis beginning with statistics for January 1962.

GOVERNMENTS.-The census of gov ernments makes available detailed basic data regarding numbers and characteristics of governmental units, public employment and payrolls, tax valuations, and governmental finances (taxes and other revenue, expenditure, indebtedness and debt transactions, and financial assets), by type of government. 

Current reports on State and local governments provide statistics principally as to their finances and employment. Statistics published annually on these subjects include nationwide figures by type of government, Stateand-local government totals by States, and comparative figures for each of the State governments and each city and town of 50,000 inhabitants or more.

An additional annual series provides data on the financial operations of employee-retirement systems administered by State and local governments. 

CONSTRUCTION.-Data are compiled monthly on housing starts (nonfarm and total), value of new construction put in place, new dwelling units authorized by local building permits in each of more than 3,000 permit-issuing jurisdictions, and national and other aggregates of new residential construction authorized in permit-issuing places. A survey to measure quarterly expenditures for residential additions, alterations, and repairs was made available on a continuing basis beginning with 1960 data. A survey to measure rate of sales and unsold inventory of new houses was initiated in March 1962. 

INTERNATIONAL STATISTICS.-Under arrangements with the Agency for In ternational Development and the De partment of State, the Bureau provides statistical consultation to foreign governments, arranges orientation pro-

11 US C grams for foreign visitors, and trains foreign technicians who are studying census and other statistical methods.

The Catalog of United States Census 

Publications is published on a quarterly (cumulative-to-annual) basis, with monthly supplements. 

The Bureau also makes special tabulations for private individuals and organizations at the cost of providing such services. In addition, searches are made of the decennial census records of population on file in the Bureau's Pittsburg, Kans., office. The data reported on these records are furnished to individuals in accordance with provisions of the law for use as evidence of age and place of birth, for obtaining employment, social-security benefits, oldage assistance, passports, naturalization papers, delayed birth certificates, and for other purposes. 

Coast and Geodetic Survey  Reg ulations, Title 33, Chapter III]  

Coast and Geodetic Survey was established as the Coast Survey by the act of February 10, 1807 (2 Stat. 413), and was redesignated by the act of 

June 20, 1878 (20 Stat. 206, 215).

Extension of geodetic work across the country was provided for by the act of 

March 3, 1871 (16 Stat. 508). Subsequent legislation charged the agency with investigations and reports on earthquakes (43 Stat. 802) and the compilation and publication of aeronautical charts of the civil airways (44 

Stat. 571). The act of August 6, 1947 (61 Stat. 788, as amended, 74 Stat. 

16; 33 U.S.C. 883a-883i), which repeals most of the previous authorizing legislation, sets forth the duties of the Coast and Geodetic Survey as regards surveys and other functions and further authorizes the agency to conduct developmental work for the improvement of surveying and cartographic methods, instruments, and equipment; to conduct investigations and research in geophysical sciences; to enter into cooperative agreements with any State, public, or private organization, or individual, for surveys or investigations; and to act as the central depository of the United States

Government for the collection of geomagnetic data from domestic and foreign sources.

PURPOSE AND FUNCTIONS.-To pro vide charts and related information for the safe navigation of marine and air commerce, and to provide basic data for engineering and scientific purposes for the development of natural resources and for other commercial and industrial needs, the Coast and Geodetic Survey conducts the following activities: (1) hydrographic, oceanographic, and topographic surveys; (2) the establishment of a primary network of horizontal and vertical control along the coasts and in the interior of the country, to coordinate the coastal surveys and provide a framework for mapping and other engineering work; and research involving the figure of the earth; (3) tidal observations and investigations to provide basic data required for vertical control of surveying and mapping operations, coastal engineering projects, and aids to navigation such as tide tables, current tables, and tidal current charts; (4) observations and research of the earth's magnetism in all parts of the country, to furnish magnetic information essential to the mariner, aviator, land surveyor, radio engineer, and others; (5) seismological observations and research to analyze destructive earthquake motions; (6) gravimetric and astronomical observations to provide fundamental data for geodetic surveys and for scientific investigations and research involving the figure of the earth; and (7) field surveys for aeronautical charting and compilation of airport obstruction charts.

ORGANIZATION.-The Coast and 

Geodetic Survey consists of the Office of the Director and the following: Of fice of Oceanography, consisting of the 

Operations Division, Facilities Divi sion, and Marine Data Division; Office of Physical Sciences, consisting of the 

Geodesy Division, Geophysics Division, Photogrammetry Division, and Elec- tronic Computing Division; Office of Research and Development; Office of Cartography, consisting of the Nautical Chart Division, Aeronautical 

Chart Division, Reproduction Divi sion, and Distribution Division; and 

Office of Administration, consisting of the Budget and Finance Division, Ad ministrative and Technical Services

Division, Personnel and Safety Divi sion, Management and Audit Division, and Instrument Division.

Office of Foreign Commercial Services The Office of Foreign Commercial 

Services was established by the Secretary of Commerce on February 1, 1963, by Department Order 183, to carry out the Department's responsibilities relating to foreign commercial services and commercial officer representation abroad. In addition, it administers the 

State-Commerce Agreement for improving overseas commercial services. 

Bureau of International Commerce  Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapters III and IX] The Bureau of International Com merce was established by the Secretary of Commerce on February 1, 1963, by 

Department Order 182 pursuant to the

Secretary's authority under Reorganization Plan 5 of 1950, effective May 24, 1950, to plan and operate the international action programs of the Department under the direction of the 

Assistant Secretary for Domestic and 

International Business. 

The Bureau of International Commerce is the center of international commercial activities in the Department. Its objectives are the creation and maintenance of a favorable trading climate overseas, the stimulation and expansion of U.S. foreign trade, the provision of media through which U.S. goods can be introduced abroad (such as trade fairs, trade missions and trade centers), and the provision of marketing and economic information for exporters and investors. The Bureau stimulates investment in lessdeveloped countries and invites foreign investors to participate in the economic growth of the United States. It also administers the Export Control and China Trade Acts. 

In cooperation with the Department of State, the Bureau utilizes the services of commercial officers in our embassies abroad to assist American traders in their efforts to expand commerce and to protect their interests when in jeopardy.

The Bureau comprises the Office of the Director, which includes the International Organizations Staff, the

Foreign Trade Zones Executive Sec retariat, the Advisory Committee on 

Export Policy Executive Secretariat, the Export Control Compliance Com missioner, and the offices described below.

FOREIGN TRADE ZONES BOARD EXECU- TIVE SECRETARIAT.-This office con ducts day-by-day regulatory, administrative, and technical affairs of the 

Foreign Trade Zones Board as required by the Foreign Trades Zones Act (48 

Stat. 998, 64 Stat. 246; 19 U.S.C. 81a, 81c). Foreign Trade Zones are in operation in New York, Louisiana, California, Washington, Ohio, and

Puerto Rico. 

OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATION.-This 

Office is responsible for all management and administrative activities which include promoting management improvement programs; formulating, developing, and administering budget and fiscal policies and programs; organizational planning and staffing; personnel management; career development; training; and general office services. 

OFFICE OF PUBLICATIONS AND INFOR- MATION.—This Office increases world-

Off 5.0 wide sales of U.S. goods by consistent inquiry into, and effective reporting of, international marketing news and potentially profitable international trading opportunities directed to the whole U.S. business community of individuals, small and large companies, and industrial associations and groups of businessmen, through periodicals, special publications, and direct communications.

OFFICE OF COMMERCIAL AND FINAN- CIAL POLICY.-This Office plans and develops the Department's international economic policies and programs. 

It prepares for and participates in negotiations for the reduction of tariffs and the elimination of nontariff barriers to trade through such multilateral mechanisms as the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). It analyzes and designs legislative and other proposals to expand U.S. foreign trade on a nondiscriminatory basis, and directs attention to particular import problems which may threaten established U.S. industries.

Through participation in staff activity for the National Advisory Council on International Monetary and Financial Problems, it shares in the establishment of general policies affecting public international lending and in the review of particular loan proposals. 

It further participates in forming U.S. procurement policies, foreign aid programs, and especially export financing and export credit insurance programs sponsored and supported by the U.S. Government. 

It coordinates for the Department business needs and broad U.S. policy aims in the development of policies and actions in the fields of restrictive business practices; U.S. and foreign tax burdens and incentives; protection of industrial property rights; and arbitrary or discriminatory treatment by foreign governments of American firms operating abroad. 

Procedures and activities are developed and recommended to expand 

American transportation and insurance interest abroad. The Office analyzes discriminatory, protectionist, and other restrictive regulations and practices prejudicial to U.S. transportation and insurance interests and their affiliates abroad, and proposes appropriate action. It provides the secretariat and and operational support to the National Facilitation Committee, which develops and carries out a comprehensive interagency program for facilitating the movement of persons and goods in international trade and travel through reduction or elimination of burdensome border-crossing formalities. It analyzes and makes policy recommendations respecting restrictive insurance legislation and practices in less developed countries in connection with expanding operations abroad of U.S. insurance companies, the placement of insurance on U.S. exports and imports, and the insurance of U.S. investments abroad. 

OFFICE OF INTERNATIONAL REGIONAL ECONOMICS.This Office has four major responsibilities: (a) to program and coordinate the Department's trade expansion program in individual countries and regions; (b) to assist individual U.S. firms and industries in dealing with their problems of doing business abroad; (c) to analyze overseas economic developments and provide information to the American business community on significant developments affecting U.S. economic interests; and (d) to recommend departmental policy with respect to individual countries and regions.

In the trade expansion program, the 

Office programs and coordinates trade. missions, trade fairs and other promotional projects for individual countries; schedules and staffs domestic trade conferences dealing with trade potentials in overseas areas; correlates the commercial staffing of Foreign Service posts and establishes programs of de-

partmental activity relating to individual countries and areas for the guidance and promotion of U.S. commercial interests. 

The country specialists provide information on marketing, investment, and economic conditions abroad; collect, analyze, and disseminate foreign. trade statistics; and identify marketing opportunities and make representations on behalf of U.S. interests abroad when difficulties arise as a result of foreign government action. The Of fice maintains information on tariff rates and regulations abroad and prepares material for and assists in tariff negotiations; identifies nontariff trade barriers and arranges for bilateral negotiations to reduce them; and participates in interdepartmental and international conferences on trade and investment problems. 

Informational and advisory services are carried on through publication in 

International Commerce and Overseas

Business Reports (formerly World 

Trade Information Service), through correspondence, consultations in Washington and in the field, and participation in trade and industry meetings. 

OFFICE OF EXPORT CONTROL.-This 

Office is concerned primarily with safeguarding the national security by regulating exports of strategic commodities to unfriendly destinations and otherwise carrying out the foreign policy of the United States. This latter purpose has assumed increasing importance by virtue of the continuing turmoil throughout the world.

OFFICE OF INTERNATIONAL INVEST- MENT.-This Office identifies profit able investment opportunities in the developing countries and brings them to the attention of U. S. business. This work is done in close cooperation with commercial officers in U. S. embassies abroad and with the Agency for In ternational Development. Licensing of 

U. S. manufacturing processes abroad and joint-ventures by American and foreign partners stimulate U. S. exports of machinery, equipment, and components, and serve our national objective jective of of accelerating economic growth in the less developed countries of the free world.

This Office also seeks to encourage firms abroad to make direct investments in the United States, especially in areas of heavy unemployment. Office provides 

OFFICE OF INTERNATIONAL TRADE PROMOTION.-This services to American business in support of the export expansion effort by planning, promoting, and operating three overseas media: trade centers, trade fair exhibits, and trade missions. 

The Office plans and conducts an international trade fair exhibits program designed to sell U. S. goods abroad. 

Its commercial intelligence program provides provides comprehensive marketing data to U. S. exporters. as 

Trade Fair Exhibits.-Beginning in fiscal year 1963, exhibits in established trade fairs have been designed to attract new firms into the export mar kets and to increase the exports of firms now in international trade. Based on market studies, the fair locations are chosen to present the highest possible export potential for U. S. goods. 

Firms are encouraged to participate by the provision of specialized design and exhibit services, along with efforts to assist them to obtain agents and distributors and to make export sales. Trade Centers.-Conceived showrooms for smaller American manufacturers, trade centers are designed to provide opportunities for businesses without international representation to show their wares and to negotiate with agents, distributors, and larger buyers to handle their goods abroad. Unlike the trade fair exhibits, the centers are permanent installations within which the products of one particular industry or commodity group are shown with different exhibits occuring 8 to 10 times a year per center. 

The four centers are located in London, Tokyo, Bangkok, and Frankfurt.

Trade Missions.-Groups of na tionally recognized industrial special-

LOT ists have completed over 115 missions to countries all over the world. These volunteers, accompanied by Department of Commerce officials, carry abroad hundreds of specific business proposals submitted in advance by U.S. manufacturers. The missions return with similar proposals from abroad for 

American businessmen. Then they tour the United States to bring the opportunities to American firms which can take advantage of them.

Interagency Trade Fair Exhibits 

Program (in cooperation with State and USIA). The primary objective of this program, consisting of about 17 exhibits either in established international trade fairs or "solo" U.S. exhibitions, is to tell the story of U.S. private enterprise in areas where the commercial potential is insufficient for a 

Commerce trade fair. Less developed countries and Soviet bloc countries are the primary sites for interagency fairs. 

Where export sales can be promoted, however, the exhibits are chosen to display salable merchandise. Each exhibit is planned around themes which take advantage of our broad variety of manufacturing enterprise to tell a story which is understandable to the people of the country in which the exhibition occurs.

Commercial Intelligence Program.-Detailed information on foreign distributors, importers, and agents is submitted by the Foreign Service, and classified, analyzed, and distributed to U.S. firms seeking representation or customers abroad.

A service conducted in cooperation with the Foreign Service provides help to American businessmen in trade complaint problems.

A detailed index of American exporters is collected on punch cards, for use in assisting American firms to take advantage of trade opportunities, and to assist the Foreign Service to channel trade leads to appropriate organizations. Maritime Administration 

(General Accounting Office Building, 441 G Street NW.) 

 Reg ulations, Title 32A, Chapter XVIII; Title 46, Chapter II] 

The Maritime Administration was established by Reorganization Plan 21 of 1950, effective May 24, 1950, as one of the successor agencies to the former United States Maritime Commission. It is headed by a Maritime 

Administrator, who is appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, and acts under authorities delegated by the Secretary of Commerce.

The Maritime Administration is responsible for administering programs authorized by the Merchant Marine Act, 1936, as amended, and related shipping statutes, to aid in the development, promotion, and operation of an American merchant marine adequate to carry the Nation's domestic waterborne commerce and a substantial portion of its foreign commerce during peacetime, and capable of serving as a naval and military auxiliary in time of war or national emergency. In carrying out its functions the 

Administration is guided by the Declaration of Policy contained in title I of the Merchant Marine Act, 1936, as amended. 

MARITIME SUBSIDY BOARD.-Under 

Reorganization Plan 7 of 1961, effective August 12, 1961, the functions of the former Federal Maritime Board, with respect to subsidization of the American merchant marine, were transferred to the Secretary of Commerce. The Secretary, in turn, established within the Maritime Adminis-

tration a Maritime Subsidy Board and delegated to it the authority to award, amend, and terminate contracts for ship construction and ship operatingdifferential subsidies, which are granted to U.S. citizens to meet disparities between United States and foreign costs in these respective areas. 

In this connection, the Maritime

Subsidy Board investigates and determines the relative cost of constructing ships in the United States and in foreign countries, and of operating ships under United States and competitive foreign flags, and takes other actions necessary to the award of subsidies and taking delegated actions antecedent thereto.

OTHER GOVERNMENT AIDS TO SHIP- PING. The Maritime Administration provides other aids to merchant shipping by insuring mortgages and/or loans made by private lending institutions to finance the construction, reconstruction, and reconditioning of ships; acquires old ships in exchange for more modern ships or for allowances of credit on the construction of new ships; and recommends to the Department of the Navy the payment of the cost of national defense features added to ships. 

The Administration also investigates and determines ocean services, routes, and lines essential for the development and maintenance of the foreign commerce of the United 

States; and the type, size, speed, and other requirements of ships to provide adequate service on such routes. The operators who are awarded operatingdifferential subsidy contracts are required to maintain regular services on these routes. 

RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT.- The Maritime Administration con ducts research and development activities in the maritime field, including cargo handling, development and utilization of new ship designs, marine transportation systems, advanced propulsion concepts, and ship management techniques. The objectives of this program are to improve the efficiency and economy of operations of the American merchant marine and to assure that it will be composed of the best-equipped, safest, and most suitable types of ships. 

SHIPBUILDING AND DESIGN.-The 

Maritime Administration develops plans and specifications for prototype ships, encourages and participates in the development of plans and designs by subsidized operators under their replacement programs, and by applicants for Government aid covering ships proposed to be constructed or converted. 

It inspects ships during the course of work to assure conformance with approved plans and specifications. It develops plans and specifications for propulsion systems and equipment, including those for the utilization of steam, diesel, and gas turbines and those involving the adaptation of nuclear power to merchant ships. To carry out the national maritime policy, the 

Maritime Administration, with the approval of the President, constructs, reconstructs, and reconditions ships for 

Government account. The Adminis tration is authorized to sell these ships, charter them to private operators, or utilize them for Government operation. 

SHIP OPERATIONS AND REPAIR.- The Maritime Administration charters 

Government-owned ships to United 

States operators when it is determined that such charters will promote the national maritime policy. During national emergencies it requisitions or procures for operation or for charter ships owned by citizens of the United States or under construction, and it determines requirements for and allocates ships to meet the needs of national defense programs. In connection with the foregoing the Maritime 

Administration prescribes ship operations and ship repair standards and administers such standards under the provisions of charter and general agency agreements and operatingdifferential subsidy contracts.

LATT LIDIANT 

NATIONAL 

FLEET.-The Maritime Administra tion maintains national defense reserve fleets of Government-owned ships determined by the Maritime Administration and the Department of Defense to be essential for national defense. Ships determined to be nonessential for national defense purposes are sold or otherwise disposed of.

DEFENSE RESERVE OPERATION OF WAREHOUSES.-The Maritime Administration maintains and operates five warehouses for the storage of marine equipment required for the reactivation, repair, and operation of ships.

RESERVE SHIPYARD.-The Maritime 

Administration maintains a shipyard in an inactive condition to be used for ship construction in national emergencies. 

MARITIME TRAINING.-The Maritime Administration operates the U. S. 

Merchant Marine Academy, Kings 

Point, N. Y. Academy graduates are licensed as merchant marine officers and qualified for commissions as en signs in the U. S. Naval Reserve. The 

Administration also administers a grant-in-aid program for State marine and nautical schools.

CONSTRUCTION RESERVE FUNDS.- 

Under regulations jointly issued by the 

Secretary of Commerce and the Secre tary of the Treasury, American shipowners may deposit proceeds from the sale or loss of ships and earnings from operation of ships in tax-deferred funds, for use in the construction or acquisition of new ships.

TRANSFER OF SHIPS TO ALIENS.- The Maritime Administration regu lates the sales to aliens, and transfers to foreign registry, of ships owned in whole or in part by citizens of the 

United States and documented under the laws of the United States, and, in time of war or national emergency, of ships so owned without regard to documentation. 

WAR RISK INSURANCE.- -The Mari time Administration is authorized to provide Government war risk insurance of merchant ships when adequate insurance cannot be obtained on reasonable terms and conditions from private insurance companies of the 

United States.

NATIONAL SHIPPING AUTHORITY.- 

The Maritime Administrator is also vested with the residual powers and authorities of the Director, National
