"Patent Office 

[For regulations Codified under this heading, see Code of Federal Reg ulations, Title 37, Chapter I]  patent Office was established to administer the patent laws enacted by Congress in accordance with Article I, section 8, of the Constitution. The first of these laws was enacted April 10, 1790 

(1 Stat. 109), but the Patent Office as a distinct bureau in the Department of State dates from 1802. General revisions of the patent laws were made on 

July 4, 1836 (5 Stat. 117), and on 

July 8, 1870 (16 Stat. 198). These and other acts of Congress relating to patents were revised and codified, effective 

January 1, 1953, by the act of July 19, 1952 (66 Stat. 792; 35 U.S.C. 1-293).

On April 1, 1925, the Patent Office was transferred from the Department of the Interior, where it had functioned since 1849, to the Department of 

Commerce by Executive Order 4175 of March 17, 1925. In addition to the patent laws, the Patent Office administers the Federal trademark laws, the present statute being the act approved July 5, 1946 (60 Stat. 427; 15

U.S.C. 1051). 

OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PATENTS.-The Office of the Commis sioner includes the Commissioner of 

Patents, the First Assistant Commissioner, and two Assistant Commissioners, one of whom is designated Assistant Commissioner for Research.

This office is responsible for formulating the policies, developing and coordinating the programs, and directing all operations, research, and administrative functions of the Patent Office. The 

First Assistant Commissioner and the 

Assistant Commissioners perform such duties pertaining to the Office of the Commissioner as may be assigned them by the Commissioner. By statutory designation they are members of the 

Board of Appeals. The functions of the immediate Office of the Commissioner are conducted by three components of that office, as follows:

Office of the Solicitor.-This Office handles all litigation to which the Commissioner is a party and all other required legal services, including advice and assistance on legislative matters. 

Office of Legislative Planning- 

This Office makes studies and advises the Commissioner on matters which may require legislative action and, with advice and assistance of the Solicitor, prepares necessary legislation and supporting reports. It also makes studies and advises the Commissioner on international patent matters. 

Office of Planning and Program Evaluation. This Office generates and develops overall Patent Office plans and evaluates the effectiveness of various segments of the Patent Office in their implementation of these plans. 

FIRST ASSISTANT COMMISSIONER.- 

The First Assistant Commissioner is in charge of all patent examining activities, with the Chairman of the 

Board of Appeals, the Board of Patent 

Interferences, and the Superintendent of the Patent Examining Corps reporting directly to him.

Board of Appeals.-This Board con sists of the Commissioner, the Assistant Commissioners, not more than fifteen examiners-in-chief, and such pro tempore members as may be assigned by the Commissioner under the authority contained in section 7 of title 35, U.S. Code. It is responsible for conducting hearings and rendering decisions on appeals from adverse decisions of examiners as to the patentability of inventions claimed in patent applications. 

Board of Patent Interferences.- 

This Board conducts patent interference proceedings and makes final determination in the Patent Office as to priority of invention. The Board also conducts proceedings and makes final determinations in the Patent Office re-

LIDNANT specting the right of the Atomic Energy

Commission and of the Administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space 

Administration to take title to certain applications and patents. Three examiners of patent interferences constitute a board of patent interferences in determining each question of priority or of title. 

Patent Examining Corps.-The Pat ent Examining Corps is directed by a 

Superintendent who is responsible to the First Assistant Commissioner for the conduct of the patent examining function. The Superintendent formulates and directs the execution of basic examining policies and practices, applies provisions of law relating to the security of applications, renders decisions on procedural and substantive matters, and exercises overall responsibility for the professional competence and productive efficiency of the examining corps. 

The Patent Examining Corps comprises an Office of Examining Con trol and four examining operations, namely: Chemical Examining Opera tion, Électrical Examining Operation,

Mechanical Engineering Examining 

Operation, and General Engineering and Industrial Arts Examining Opera tion. The respective groups are headed by a Supervisory Examiner who is responsible to the Director of the appropriate Examining Operation.

The Office of Examining Control develops procedures and quality and quantity standards relating to the conduct of the examining function; evaluates examiner compliance with such standards; trains new examiners in patent practice and procedure, oper ating the Patent Office Academy for this purpose; and issues instructions regarding all procedures relating to the patent examining function. 

ASSISTANT COMMISSIONER. The 

Assistant Commissioner is in charge of all trademark examining activities with the Trademark Trial and Appeal 

Board and the Director of the Trademark Examining Operation reporting to him. He also has supervision of the Office of Administration and the Office of Information Services with their respective directors responsible to him.

Trademark Trial and Appeal 

Board. This Board is responsible for hearing and deciding adversary proceedings involving interfering applications, oppositions to registration, cancellation petitions, and concurrent use proceedings, and for hearing and deciding appeals from final refusals of the trademark examiners to allow the registration of trademarks. 

Trademark Examining Operation.- 

This activity is responsible for conducting the trademark examining and trademark classification functions of the Patent Office. The Director, Trademark Examining Operation, formulates and directs the execution of basic examination and classification policies and practices relating to the registration of marks; insures that such policies comply with statutory and regulatory provisions, court decisions, and decisions of the Commissioner; and effects standards of performance.

The functions of the principal organizational units of the Trademark 

Examining Operation are described below. 

The Trademark Examining Divi sions, cach under the supervision of a primary examiner, examine applications for the registration of marks within assigned classes of goods or services. They develop the formal sufficiency of applications; determine the registrable merits of marks through search of the prior registrations and application of references, precedent decisions, established rules and procedures, and statutory requirements; allow or reject applications on the basis of their findings; record abandonments; and institute interference proceedings for determining the right to register and rule on motions in connection therewith.

The Trademark Classification and 

Search Division develops and main-

tains a system for the classification of goods and services to which marks may be applied; insures the effective application of the system in the examination of applications and the registration of marks; and maintains a digest of registered, published, and pending marks, classified according to the characteristics of the marks, to facilitate reference searches by examiners and the public. 

Office of Administration.-The Di rector of this Office formulates and directs the execution of administrative policies and programs. In this capacity he supervises budget and fiscal operations, personnel administration, and management review and improvement. 

He is also responsible to the Assistant 

Commissioner for directing and coordinating the nonexamining services of the Patent Office, which include the review of new patent applications for compliance with formal requirements prior to consideration by patent examiners, preparation of allowed applications for printing, recording assignments of patent and trademark rights, sale of printed copies of patents and trademarks, maintaining dockets of inter partes patent cases and court appeals, providing punch card accounting and documentation services, and providing copies of Patent Office records.

Office of Information Services.- 

The Director of this Office advises and represents the Commissioner on public information matters and conducts information programs fostering public knowledge of and benefit from the 

American patent system and the functions and services of the Patent Office. 

ASSISTANT COMMISSIONER FOR RE- SEARCH.-The Assistant Commissioner for Research has charge of the Office of Research and Development, the 

Office of Patent Classification, and the

Scientific Library, the heads of which are responsible to him.

Office of Research and Develop ment. This Office, which is headed by a Director of Research, conducts research on the organization of information for novelty searching and develops retrieval systems, including computer-assisted systems, for the use of information by Patent Office examiners and the scientific community.

Office of Patent Classification.- 

This Office is responsible for developing a system for the classification of patents in the various useful arts and insuring the effective use of this system in the classification of issued patents. The classification provides a basic reference source for making use of patents in searches for novelty, interference, or infringement of invention. The Office is headed by a Supervisory Classification Examiner.

Scientific Library.-The Scientific 

Library is responsible for obtaining and bringing pertinent technical and scientific information to the attention of patent and trademark examiners and in interested segments of the public. It contains over 110,000 scientific and technical books, over 73,000 bound volumes of periodicals devoted to science and technology, the official journals of foreign patent offices, and more than 7 million copies of patents issued by foreign countries. A public search room, containing numerical and classified sets of patents, is maintained for use of the public in searching and examining U.S. patents and their records. 

Publications.-When patents are granted, printed copies of the specifications and drawings are prepared and published. Copies of over three million patents are kept in stock for distribution and sale to the public. 

Trademarks registered are similarly published. The Patent Office also publishes an Official Gazette which appears weekly, annual indexes of patents and trademarks, annual volumes of decisions in patent and trademark cases, a manual of classification, a manual of patent examining procedure, classification bulletins, rules of practice, compilations of patent laws, trademark laws and rules, and pamphlets of general information.

United States Travel Service CREATION. The United States 

Travel Service was established June 

29, 1961, pursuant to the International

Travel Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 129; 22 

U.S.C. 2121 note) as a primary organization unit in the Department of Commerce. 

PURPOSE. The purposes of the 

'Travel Service are to develop, plan, and carry out a comprehensive program designed to stimulate and encourage travel to the United States by residents of foreign countries for the purpose of study, culture, recreation, business, and other activities as a means of promoting friendly understanding and good will among peoples of foreign countries and of the United States; encourage the development of tourist facilities, low-cost unit tours, and other arrangements within the United States for meeting the requirements of foreign visitors; foster and encourage the widest possible distribution of the benefits of travel at the cheapest rates between foreign countries and the United States consistent with sound economic principles; encourage the simplification, reduction, or elimination of barriers. to travel, and the facilitation of international travel generally; collect, publish, and provide for the exchange of statistics and technical information, including schedules of meetings, fairs, and other attractions, relating to international travel and tourism.

ORGANIZATION.-The program of the Travel Service is conducted by the following divisions: Sales Promotion, Media Relations, Facilitation and 

Planning, and Visitor Services. In addition to these divisions, nine overseas offices have been established to stimulate tourist travel. These offices are located in London, England; Paris, France; Frankfurt, Germany; Tokyo, Japan; Sydney, Australia; São Paulo, Brazil; Bogotá, Colombia; Rome, Italy; and Mexico City, Mexico.

ACTIVITIES.-The major share of ap propriated funds are used to provide tools and materials for distribution by the overseas offices, such as advertisements, pamphlets, brochures, posters, slides, and films, in order to help the prospective traveler study and measure the United States against other competitive destinations. 

In addition, the following activities are being carried out: editorial support of the program through domestic and foreign media endorsing the 

United States as a tourist destination; 201

el 2015 encouragement to State and local community groups for the establishment of "host" services throughout the country; development of ways and means of overcoming barriers to travel; and a study of the economic aspects of tourism and patterns of international travel. 

National Bureau of Standards 

(Connecticut Avenue at Van Ness Street NW.; EMerson 2-4040)  Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter II] The National Bureau of Standards was established by act of Congress of March 3, 1901 (31 Stat. 1449 as amended; 15 U. S. C. 271-286).

The Bureau was initially part of the 

Treasury Department and was transferred to the Department of Commerce and Labor on its creation in 1903. 

PURPOSE. -The fundamental purpose of the National Bureau of Standards is to provide national leadership in the development and use of accurate and uniform techniques of physical measurement. With leadership in physical measurement as the focus, the scientific activity of NBS has three major components: (1) provision of the central basis within the United States of a complete and consistent system of physical measurement, and coordination of that system with the measurement systems of other nations; (2) provision of essential services leading to accurate and uniform physical measurement throughout the Nation's science, industry, and commerce, and consonant with their advancing requirements; and (3) provision of data on the properties of matter and materials which are of importance to science, industry, and commerce, and which are not available of sufficient accuracy elsewhere. This purpose derives from the statutory responsibility to develop and maintain the national standards for physical measurement, to provide means for their effective utilization, and to determine physical constants and properties of materials of importance to science and industry. Measurement standards are provided for such quantities as length, mass, time, volume, temperature, light, color, electrical energy, radioactivity, X-ray intensity, viscosity, sound, radio frequency, and many others.

The Bureau serves as the contact point of the Federal Government for the exchange of standards with other governments, and participates in developing new and more precise international standards of measurement. 

Also, it provides standards for the States within the United States as they may require and request.

Additional functions include the development of methods of test, the testing of materials, cooperation with other governmental and private organizations in the establishment of codes and specifications, advisory service to other Government agencies on scientific and technical problems and the invention and development of devices to serve the special needs of these agencies. 

The Bureau provides a central Federal technical service in a number of specialized areas, a major example being the operation of the Central Radio 

Propagation Laboratory. 

ORGANIZATION.-The scientific and technical program of the Bureau is conducted by the following divisions: 

Analytical and Inorganic Chemistry, Applied Mathematics, Atomic Physics, Building Research, Cryogenic Engineering, Data Processing Systems,

Electricity, Heat, Inorganic Solids, Ionosphere Research and Propagation, Instrumentation, Laboratory Astro-

physics Group, Mechanics, Metallurgy, Metrology, Office of Weights and 

Measures, Physical Chemistry, Poly mers, Troposphere and Space Telecommunications, Radiation Physics,

Radio Systems, Radio Standards En gineering, Radio Standards Physics, and Upper Atmosphere and Space 

Physics. 

The Bureau's radio and cryogenic engineering laboratories are located at 

Boulder, Colo. Various field stations. are concerned with radio investigations, with the calibration of railway track scales, and with the testing of materials. or individuals engaged in pursuits requiring the use of standards. The testing of products for performance, however, is confined mainly to Federal agencies; for others the Bureau will occasionally do testing if there are no facilities available elsewhere. 

ACTIVITIES. A broad program of fundamental research in physics, chemistry, mathematics, and engineering is conducted in order to lay the ground work for new standards and to provide means and methods for making comparisons and calibrations with the ever increasing accuracy required by science and industry. Much of this research is directly concerned with the accurate measurement of pure substances and the properties of materials of importance to industry and commerce.

Many standards are disseminated most effectively through the preparation and distribution of standard samples of pure substances or industrial materials, the composition and properties of which have been accurately determined. 

The testing, calibration, and certification of standards and standard measuring apparatus are a service. that the Bureau renders broadly, not only for the Federal Government and State and municipal governments, but also for scientific societies, educational institutions, and firms Advisory functions include consultative services to other Government agencies and dissemination of scientific and technical data through publications and reports, and through technical conferences. In addition to assistance in the preparation of specifications for Federal purchase by agencies of the Government, the Bureau assists States, municipalities, industry, and universities in developing methods of measurement. 

The Bureau serves as the coordinat- རུ ། འ། ad ing agency to bring together the State officials of weights and measures and other regulatory agencies for national conferences and committee activities, and prepares advisory documents as model codes and digests of existing codes to assist in the formulation of uniform and compatible regulations for building safety, electrical devices, weights and measures, and other reg ulations related to physical properties. 

Weather Bureau (M Street between Twenty-fourth and Twenty-fifth Streets NW.; telephone, 965-2400)  

Regulations, Title 15, Chapter V] 

The national weather service was established in 1870 under the Signal 

Corps of the Army. By act of October 

1, 1890 (26 Stat. 653; 15 U. S. C. 311), the Weather Bureau was organized under the Department of Agriculture, and on July 1, 1891, the weather service was transferred to it from the Gulf MRI Cen 

Signal Corps. Subsequent legislation and Executive decisions have greatly increased the Bureau's responsibilities, especially in providing weather service for civil aviation. The President's Reorganization Plan IV transferred the

Bureau to the Department of Commerce, effective June 30, 1940.

WAND LAW LIDIANT 

Weather stations in the Arctic are maintained under authority of the act of May 12, 1946 (60 Stat. 4; 15 U.S.C. 313a). 

The Weather Bureau maintains about 300 offices, manned by full-time personnel, at cities and airports throughout the United States and in 

Puerto Rico and some of the islands of the Pacific Ocean. The local offices of the Bureau make surface and upper air weather measurements required for weather forecasting; maintain records and transmit reports; and where appropriate issue local forecasts and warnings. 

In addition, weather reports are made at about 675 other locations by personnel of certain other Government agencies, notably the Federal Aviation 

Agency, State and municipal groups, airlines, and private citizens. 

For administrative purposes, the supervision of field stations is exercised through 5 regional administrative offices and the Pacific Supervisory

Office. 

In cooperation with the Coast 

Guard, the U.S. Navy, and certain maritime interests, the Weather Bureau maintains ocean weather stations in both the Atlantic and the Pacific and in the Gulf of Mexico.

WEATHER SERVICES.-The Weather 

Bureau maintains a National Meteorological Center at Suitland, Md., which analyzes weather conditions over the northern hemisphere, prepares guidance prognostic material and disseminates it via facsimile and other rapid communication media to both civil and military forecast offices to support their weather service activities.

Severe Local Storm Forecasting Cen ter at Kansas City prepares special forecasts for tornadoes, etc., to augment the radar and volunteer networks maintained by local offices to provide warning service.

The 

A general weather service comprising daily weather bulletins, forecasts, warnings, and advices for the public, agriculture, business, commerce, industry, and other interests is provided through field stations of the Weather

Bureau. This information is localized for the area of responsibility assigned to each office, based upon the area forecasts issued from 28 forecast centers. Forecasts are available four times daily to cover weather developments expected during the ensuing 36 to 48 hours. In critical situations warnings of storms and cold waves are issued as conditions warrant, without regard to regular forecasting schedules. 

Weather bulletins and forecasts are published by nearly all daily newspapers and broadcast by most commercial radio and television stations in the country. More than 250 radio stations maintain microphones in Weather Bureau offices for direct use by Bureau personnel to make weather information service widely available to the general public. Local communication companies have established Public Service 

Weather Teletypewriter Circuits in about 90 cities of the country for the primary distribution of weather information to mass news disseminators. In turn, the dissemination of this information to the general public is accomplished much more rapidly. The automatic telephone forecast repeater, installed and maintained by the operating telephone company in 12 major cities, has proved a popular service, averaging about 50,000 calls daily per installation with a record of 477,148 calls in one day at one such installation. 

Five-day weather outlook statements are issued for all parts of the 

United States 3 times weekly. A 30day outlook is issued at Washington twice a month.

The Aviation Weather Service op erates 24 hours every day to supply information and weather forecasts for air operations in the United States and over transocean routes. The domestic service consists of about 250 airport stations, connected by FAA teletypewriter circuits, which collect and exchange detailed reports hourly on weather conditions along the civil

airways, and disseminate forecasts and other current weather information. 

Preflight weather briefing is available at all airport stations. Operational forecasts for aviation are issued every 

6 hours by 27 Flight Advisory Weather

Service Centers. Warnings of poten tially hazardous flying weather are issued as needed for safety of aircraft in flight. Also, specially composed pilot weather briefing texts are prepared and transcribed for mass dissemination by continuous, self-repeating broadcast on FAA low frequency air navigation radio channels at 69 locations and on automatic telephone at 45 metropolitan communities over the country. 

Under agreement with foreign governments the Weather Bureau provides forecasts for many overseas air routes.

The international air routes are served by forecasting and pilot briefing services, with special attention to transoceanic and high altitude flights.

These forecasts are disseminated to international airports and interested subscribers by long-line teletypewriter and facsimile circuits. 

A horticultural protection service provides specialized warnings and forecasts on a cooperative basis in certain States where fruit and vegetable production is a major activity. In addition, an agricultural weather service has been established in 9 areas of the country to meet the requirements of farmers for weather information. 

Forecasts, warnings, summaries, and advisories are distributed to mass disseminators in the areas served over a teletypewriter network. An agricultural meteorologist works with research personnel at experiment stations on technical studies on agriculture-weather relationships and their application to farm operations. The forest fire weather service provides forecasts of humidity, wind, and thunderstorm conditions in the forested regions of the country to assist the 

United States Forest Service and other agencies (State and private) in combating the fire menace. 

The marine meteorological service collects about 1,000 weather observations daily from vessels at sea by radio and supplies bulletins comprising weather reports, forecasts, and storm warnings for broadcasts to ships under way on the oceans and the Great

Lakes. Closely related to this marine work is the hurricane warning service, which issues and distributes its highly important storm advices and warnings from special hurricane forecast centers during the critical seasons.

CLIMATOLOGICAL SERVICES. -Under the guidance of a staff office in Washington, D.C., the Climatological Service collects, publishes, and analyzes data from the 300 regular Weather 

Bureau stations and the 13,000 substations manned by cooperative observers, most of them volunteers. The processing of the data is essentially automated through the operations of the National Weather Records Center, 

Asheville, N.C. Observations are prepared for publication in regular series which cover the United States, Puerto 

Rico, and the Trust Territories. The data are available as official evidence on weather conditions in legal cases and insurance settlements. 

Analytical work to make the climatological data useful for commerce, industry, and agriculture is also carried on at the National Weather Records 

Center, Asheville, N.C. This Center is equipped with modern electronic data processing facilities. It also acts as the ultimate repository of all United

States weather data, including those collected by meteorological satellites.

Climatological information is disseminated through a field service composed of area and State climatologists.

Their function is developmental work in climatology in cooperation with universities, State organizations, and 

Chambers of Commerce. The field climatologists also collect information on severe storms and cooperate with agricultural agencies in the preparation of weekly weather and crop summaries. These are collected and

LATI LIDIANT 

are disseminated nationally through the 

Washington office.

Climatological research is directed toward the charting of all climatic elements, their time trends, the problems of droughts, the average conditions of the upper air, the development of new statistical techniques to assess climatic risks, and the use of climatic data for land use, construction, air conditioning, and air pollution.

HYDROLOGIC SERVICES.-A river and flood forecasting system operates in 90 districts covering all the principal rivers and tributaries of the United 

States. There are 13 river forecast centers or units, each responsible for a major river basin and furnishing key river forecasts to the local district offices within the basin. River stages are observed daily at about 1,500 stations and daily river stage forecasts from 24 to 72 hours in advance are made on many of the larger rivers for the benefit of river navigation and control, in addition to flood stage forecasts made as needed. The observed stages are published in an annual summary for the use of industry, commerce, water utilization, and floodcontrol interests.

In collaboration with the United 

States Corps of Engineers, the Weather

Bureau maintains and publishes data from a network of some 3,000 special precipitation measuring stations, and makes studies of outstanding storms of record to determine the maximum rainfall amounts likely to fall over river basins for which engineering works are under development. Storm characteristics and frequencies are analyzed for the Department of Agriculture watershed protection program. 

In the Western States the Bureau's network of mountain snowfall stations is used to provide forecasts of runoff from the snow fields for irrigation and other water interests, published from January to May, inclusive, in "Water Supply Forecasts for the Western United

States." 

METEOROLOGICAL SATELLITES.-As a consequence of the unparalleled success of the first several TIROS meteorological satellites the President, in 1961, requested congressional approval of a plan for the establishment and operation of a National Operational Meteorological Satellite System 

(NOMSS) which would provide for the continuous observation of worldwide meteorological conditions and for the reporting and processing of the data obtained for use in weather forecasting. 

The Weather Bureau has been designated as the managing agency for this system and is proceeding, jointly with the National Aeronautics and

Space Administration, with the construction of Command and Data Acquisition stations, procurement of spacecraft and launch vehicles, and the development and procurement of data processing and communication systems. This work is carried out by the 

National Weather Satellite Center which is also responsible for the Weather Bureau's operational and research and development activities associated with meteorological satellites.

In the first phase of NOMSS the 

Weather Bureau is purchasing TIROS 

satellites to supplement NASA's R&D 

TIROS launches. This will provide nearly continuous satellite observations until the advanced NIMBUS satellite, now being developed by NASA, becomes available for regular operational use. Data obtained from the TIROS series of satellites are being used operationally in weather analysis and forecasting as well as meteorological research. NASA plans to launch its first research and development NIMBUS satellite late in 1963; the Weather

Bureau plans to use these data operationally as a part of NOMSS. 

RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT.-The 

Weather Bureau conducts basic and applied meteorological and hydrologic research in its own laboratories and

under contract at universities and other institutions to expand the knowledge of the science of the atmosphere and to improve the services of the 

Weather Bureau.

Studies are conducted to improve both short-range and extended period forecasts, including research and development work associated with the application of high speed electronic computers in weather forecasting (numerical weather prediction).

Extensive projects for the investigation of both hurricanes and tornadoes are being conducted. The projects include the collection of surface and upper air data from special networks and from aircraft operated for research purposes. These and other data are used in research by the Weather Bureau and at colleges and universities under contract to the Weather Bureau. 

Research and development in the field of meteorological instrumentation are being conducted to find new or improved techniques for surface and upper air measurements. 

Laboratory and field research is being carried out to obtain a better understanding of the physical processes that bring about condensation and growth of cloud particles to form precipitation. Basic studies are conducted of the cooling and heating of the atmosphere and its large and small scale motions.

In conjunction with the United States space program the Weather Bureau conducts an expanding program of meteorological satellite research which includes the development of advanced meteorological satellite experiments and analysis of meteorological satellite data with the objectives of developing systems and techniques for maximum utilization of these data in operational weather analysis and forecasting, and of achieving a better understanding of basic atmospheric processes. 

PUBLICATIONS.-Research findings and materials are published in the Research Paper Series and the Monthly Weather Review, or in the journals of scientific societies. A variety of periodicals, serials, and miscellaneous publications on weather, climate, hydrology, and meteorological science is issued to disseminate technical information among meteorologists, climatologists, hydrologists, and the general public, and to make observational data and climatic summaries available to potential users. The peri- odicals include Daily Weather and 

River Bulletins, Daily Weather Map, Weekly Weather and Crop Bulletin, 

Climatological Data, Storm Data, Mariners Weather Log, Average

Monthly Weather Résumé and Out look, Monthly Weather Review, and

Daily River Stages (annual). The serials include Technical Papers, Research Papers, Hydrometeorological

Reports, Observational Manuals, Cli matography of the United States, Ter minal Forecasting Reference Manuals, and Daily Series-Synoptic Weather 

Maps. Approved.

Department of Labor, ninth executive department, was created by act ap proved March 4, 1913 (37 Stat. 

736; 5 U.S.C. 611). A Bureau of

Labor was first created by Congress in 1884 under the Interior Department. The Bureau of Labor later became independent as a Department of Labor without executive rank. It again returned to bureau status in the De partment of Commerce and Labor which was created by act of February 

14, 1903 (32 Stat. 827; 5 U. S. C. 591).

Additional duties related to the statutory functions of the Department of Labor subsequently have been assigned to the Department by new legislation and by Executive order.

PURPOSE. The Department of La bor is charged, among other things, with administering and enforcing statutes designed to advance the public interest by promoting the welfare of the wage earners of the United States, improving their working conditions, and advancing their opportunities for profitable employment.

ORGANIZATION.-All functions of the 

Department are vested in the Secretary of Labor. The structure of the 

Department is shown in the organization chart which appears on page 601. 

Secretary of Labor 

 Reg ulations, Title 29, Subtitle A] 

As head of the Department of Labor and the principal adviser to the President in the development and execution of policies and the administration and enforcement of laws relating to wage earners, their working conditions, and their opportunities for employment, the 

Secretary of Labor is charged with the responsibility for all activities of the 

Department of Labor. 

OFFICE OF LEGISLATIVE LIAISON.- 

The Director of the Office, as a Special , is authorized, on behalf of the Secretary and within the general policies established by him, to coordinate, supervise, and direct all legislative activities of the Department, including contacts with the Congress and presentation of departmental legislative programs and views to the Congress. 

OFFICE OF THE PRESIDENT'S COM- MITTEE ON EMPLOYMENT OF THE HANDICAPPED.-The Office was estab lished within the Office of the Secretary to provide facilities, staff, and services to the President's Committee in accordance with the President's letters of July 11, 1949, and May 10, 1952, and Executive Order 10994 of Febru ary 14, 1962. 

The voluntary citizens committee seeks to create a proper climate in which handicapped men and women workers can seek and find gainful employment suited to their skills and abilities. 

The Committee carries on promotional activities through Governors committees in all States, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, and the District of Columbia.

Under Secretary of Labor The Under Secretary of Labor is the alternate of the Secretary in the discharge of all the Secretary's responsibilities. He serves as Acting Secretary in the Secretary's absence. 

DEPUTY UNDER SECRETARY OF LA- BOR.-The Deputy Under Secretary assists the Secretary and the Under 

Secretary by reviewing and appraising program operations of the Depart- ANT 235 Man

WAND LAT LIDNAAT ment, seeing that policies are properly reflected in programs, and that policy objectives are achieved by program operations. He has responsibility, subject to the direction of the Under Secretary who is also the Manpower 

Administrator, for policy direction, planning, and supervision of all departmental programs and bureau activities in the areas of domestic, foreign, and migratory farm labor. He supervises the mobilization and the interdepartmental and intradepartmental committee activities of the Department, the Assistant to the Under 

Secretary (Field Operations), and the Department's historical research activities. 

OFFICE OF INFORMATION, PUBLICA- TIONS, AND REPORTS.-This office coordinates and monitors the preparation and distribution of all information dealing with the work of the Department and operates as a departmental clearinghouse for all information of value to labor, business, and to the general public. The Director of

Information, Publications, and Reports plans and directs all informational activities of the Department, advises the Secretary on the public information aspect of the Department's programs, and develops and maintains appropriate liaison with other agencies and organizations and with foreign countries in connection with the work of the Department. He oversees the dissemination of information to the public concerning the Department's activities and programs. He is responsible for adequate distribution of economic, technical, and statistical materials developed by the Department through research and analysis, and for review of materials prepared in the various offices of the Department for conformity with general policy, accuracy, and presentability. The Director supervises departmental relations with press, radio, television, and other public information media. He is clearance officer for all Labor Department releases, and determines the need and suitability of format and style of all informational publications and exhibits planned and prepared in the Department.

Manpower Administration 

The Manpower Administrator has responsibility for all the Department manpower programs and activities. He is assisted by Deputy Manpower Administrators, Assistant Manpower Administrators, and other officials having responsibility for specified functions relating to a comprehensive manpower program which includes forecasting and research, development, distribution, utilization, administration, and program support. 

The Manpower Administration is composed of the office and bureaus described in the following paragraphs. 

Office of Manpower, Automation, and Training This office performs functions of the 

Secretary of Labor in the fields of automation and manpower and under the Manpower Development and 

Training Act of 1962 (76 Stat. 25; 42 

U.S.C. 2581), and the Area Redevelopment Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 58, 59; 

42 U.S.C. 2513, 2514), worker adjustment provisions under the Trade Expansion Act (76 Stat. 892; 19 U.S.C. 

1931), and other specialized programs.

The Director is also the Deputy Manpower Administrator for Planning, Research, and Evaluation.

The Office develops and recommends plans for a comprehensive national manpower program that will guide and make possible the coordination of decisions and activities of the Department of Labor, and in addition provide guidelines for other Federal agencies, employers, labor unions, pro-

The Office appraises the manpower requirements and resources of the Nation and develops policies, objectives, and standards to deal with the problems of persistent and other types of unemployment and underemployment, while considering such factors as current and prospective manpower shortages, dislocations in the economy arising from automation or other technological developments, foreign competition, relocation of industry, shifts in market demands, and other changes in the structure of the economy. 

The Office is responsible for planning an overall program of manpower research and statistics, for conducting research, and arranging for other bureaus of the Department, other Government agencies, and private agencies to conduct research and related statistics programs. The objective is to identify the many ramifications and the dimensions of the manpower problems of the Nation and to seek through research, adequate solutions to these problems. It plans and directs developmental and experimental studies in all areas of manpower and automation to find solutions to problems. which significantly affect the Nation's ability to eliminate persistent and other types of unemployment and underemployment and to evaluate the impact of and benefits and problems created by automation and other forms of technological progress. It plans and develops a program to increase and expand knowledge of how occupational competence is achieved that will aid in eliminating unemployment and underemployment. 

The Office prepares materials for the President's and the Secretary of

Labor's Annual Manpower Reports together with recommendations for action. It provides technical manpower information to the public, professional groups, unions, employers, and Government agencies on the nature of manpower problems and programs. It maintains a clearinghouse of technical and research information on manpower, automation, and training. 

The Office coordinates the program planning and development activities of the Department of Labor bureaus

-providing manpower programs for the aging, minority groups, the handicapped and youth, and insures that the bureaus and offices providing manpower programs take into account the occupational interests, circumstances, and operations of women in the labor force. ​AR The Office is responsible for evaluating plans, programs, progress, and results of the elements of the comprehensive manpower program; examining and reporting on special difficulties which interfere with achievement of general objectives; and providing appraisals of the adequacy of programs to meet foreseeable manpower needs. 

Bureau of Apprenticeship and

Training This bureau was first established in the Department of Labor by act of 

August 16, 1937 (50 Stat. 664; 29 

U.S.C. 50). It was transferred out of the Department (see appendix A) and later returned to this Department by Executive Order 9617 of Septem ber 19, 1945. 

The Bureau provides stimulation, promotion, and technical assistance for the organization of programs to improve and broaden the skills of the work force. Services are provided to industry, management, labor, community groups, and others concerned with manpower development. Bureau activities are carried on in cooperation with State agencies similarly engaged and with vocational education authorities. 

Primary emphasis is placed upon promoting the development of skilled craftsmen through apprenticeship. In cooperation with national advisory committees appointed by the Secre tary of Labor, the Bureau formulates and recommends fundamentals of apprenticeship for training craftsmen in industry. Such fundamentals deal primarily with the welfare of the apprentice as an employed worker and with such matters as adequate work experience, length of apprenticeship, provisions for supervision, related technical instruction, wages, hours, working conditions, and employer-employee participation. The Bureau, in cooperation with State apprenticeship agencies, endeavors to extend the application of fundamentals of apprenticeship by bringing together employers and labor to formulate programs of apprenticeship, and by giving technical and

Bureau of Employment Security 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 20, Chapter V] 

The Bureau's responsibilities are related to the administration of a nationwide system of public employment services, State unemployment insurance programs, Federal unemployment compensation programs, and special manpower programs designed to relieve the effects of unemployment and to promote maximum utilization of the Nation's manpower. The legislative bases for the Bureau's operations are many, including the Wagner- Peyser Act, the Federal Unemploy ment Tax Act, titles III, IX, XII, and XV of the Social Security Act, title V 

of the Agricultural Act of 1949, and various provisions in the Immigration and Nationality Act, the Area Rede- 

velopment Act, the Manpower Development and Training Act, and the 

Trade Expansion Act. Jow for Title III of the Social Security Act and the Wagner-Peyser Act provide conditions under which a State may receive Federal grants for the administration of its unemployment insurance law and State employment service programs, The latter act imposes. certain direct operating duties on the Federal agency, to be carried out through the Bureau's United States 

Employment Service. In addition, there are conditions in the Federal Un employment Tax Act (chapter 23 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954) 

which a State law must meet in order that employers within the State may become entitled to certain credits against the Federal tax for which they are liable under that act.

Conditions for grants for the administration of State employment offices include a State's acceptance of provisions of the Wagner-Peyser Act and a plan of operation found by the 

Bureau to meet Federal requirements.

In order that a State may receive grants for the administration of its unemployment insurance program, its law must contain a number of provisions required under the Social Security Act. Conditions for approval of 

State unemployment insurance laws for purposes of normal tax offset (credit of State tax paid by an employer against the Federal tax) include provisions for safeguarding workers' rights to benefits and requirements to safeguard benefit funds. 77 The laws under which the States operate their unemployment insurance programs differ widely in coverage, in benefit provisions, in eligibility and disqualification requirements, and in systems of employer experience rating and the resulting contribution rates.

The Bureau has responsibility for (1) studying and recommending new programs and proposed revision in existing programs relating to the cur-

rent and anticipated problems and needs of both the wage earner and the employer in the labor market; (2) directly administering employment security programs as required by Federal law, or other delegated authority; (3) keeping abreast of de- 

1velopments in employment security and related fields, and coordinating employment security action with reslated activities of other bureaus of the 

Department, with other agencies of

Government, and with the public; (4) providing advisory and informational services on employment security matters to the legislative and executive branches of Government; (5) promoting understanding and acceptance of the employment security system; (6) participating in the development of plans, programs, and policies for the mobilization, allocation, and utilization of the civilian labor force under naitional emergencies; and (8) cooperating with other Federal agencies in providing training and assistance to foreign governments.

The Bureau provides leadership to the State employment security agencies, involving responsibility to: (1) develop and interpret national policies and goals; (2) study program needs and administrative problems; (3) develop techniques, tools, and measures for improvement in administration and program content; (4) promote adoption of improvements in State legislation and administration; and (5) provide continuing technical assistance and interchange of experience and information. Beyond its leadership role, the Bureau obtains and allocates funds necessary for proper and efficient administration of the employment security program in the several States and Territories, conduct ing audits of related expenditures to insure that funds have been expended for purposes allocated. Also, the Bureau is responsible for insuring conformity of State laws with requirements of Federal laws, and compliance of State administration with provisions of State laws as necessary to meet Federal legal requirements. 

The Bureau's operations cover a wide range of activities. It plans programs on a nationwide basis. To enable sound program planning, it collects and analyzes operational and economic data, which in published form provide Government, labor, management, and the public with information of value in assessing economic trends and developments. 

The Bureau conducts evaluations of the administration and operation of 

State employment security agencies. 

This involves the measurement of achievements, the making of recommendations for improving State administrative operations and management, and the provision of assistance in the establishment of improved methods of administration and operation. 

Fiscal responsibilities involve justification of appropriation requests before Congress, allocation of funds among States, establishment of standards for expenditures, auditing of State fiscal accounts and records, filing of exceptions on funds improperly expended, review of applicable State laws and their execution, and certification of such laws to enable the allocation of Federal funds for administrative costs.

The Bureau works closely with State agencies in the development and maintenance of a well-selected and trained personnel staff. It develops methods for the selection, training, and management of employment security staff. 

To obtain maximum advantage of the resources available in State employment security agencies, the Bureau coordinates nationwide developmental projects which are designed to provide tools, methods, and material for adaptive use throughout the employment security system. This coordination enables widespread research, testing, and validation of techniques. From such coordinated effort have come such

The Bureau also actively participates in mobilization planning and in the preparation being made by the Federal Government for national emergencies which might arise. In addition, the Bureau coordinates civil defense and mobilization activities in 

State employment security agencies.

The eight regional administrators of the Bureau whose offices are nearest to those of the Office of Emergency Plan ning have been given responsibility for carrying out the Department's manpower mobilization activities in the field.

These overall responsibilities are in addition to specific responsibilities for the two basic programs, as described below. 

The Bureau's employment service program responsibilities, as assigned to its United States Employment Service under the provisions of the Wagner- Peyser Act, include assistance in establishing and maintaining systems of public employment offices in the 

States; assistance in coordinating such systems throughout the country and increasing their usefulness by developing and prescribing minimum standards of efficiency; furnishing information as to opportunities for employment and other information of value in operating the systems, including information about about labor market developments by area (and classification of areas according to relative labor supply), by industry, by occupation, and for agriculture; maintaining a public employment service for the District of Columbia, a veterans' service devoted to securing employment for veterans, and a farm placement service; and maintaining a system for clearing labor among the

States. The United States Employ ment Service guides and assists the States in placement functions, occupational analysis, counseling, and testing functions; in maximizing employment opportunities for veterans, older workers, youth, handicapped workers, and members of minority groups; in promoting community efforts toward the greatest possible use of the labor force; in compiling, analyzing, and disseminating labor market information; in promoting use by employers of the public employment service; and in providing materials and techniques to employers for effective use of manpower.

The United States Employment 

Service was given additional responsibility during 1961 and 1962 under the 

Area Redevelopment Act to (1) obtain facts needed for determining eligibility of areas, (2) review manpower aspects of overall economic plans for these areas, (3) determine occupations for which training programs may be required, and (4) select and refer individuals for training; under the Man power Development and Training Act to (1) determine training needs, (2) select and refer trainees, (3) develop job opportunities, (4) refer trainees to jobs, and (5) followup placements of trainees; under the Trade Expansion

Act to assist eligible persons in finding suitable employment and in obtaining appropriate training; and under the 

Public Works Acceleration Act to (1) 

obtain facts needed to determine the areas which are eligible for assistance and (2) select and refer workers to contractors and agencies on projects. 

Under the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, the United States 

Employment Service, with the assistance of the State employment security offices, reviews and makes determinations on requests for the importation and employment of alien workers to assure that in cases approved, the alien workers will not displace, nor adversely affect the wages and working_conditions of, workers in the United States similarly employed.

Within the United States Employ ment Service, a separate organizational unit has been established for maintaining a service for veterans. 

The responsibility (including the assurance of special consideration for veterans and preferential treatment for disabled veterans in employment service activities) is carried out under title IV of the Servicemen's Readjust ment Act of 1944, as amended, and policies established by the Secretary of Labor, through the Veterans Employment Service of the United

States Employment Service, operating through veterans employment representatives assigned to each of the States and Territories to collaborate with the employment security agency. They have functional responsibility for supervising the registration of veterans. in local employment offices and for placing veterans in employment; they assist in obtaining and maintaining current information as to available employment, promote the interest of employers in employing veterans, maintain regular contact with employers and veterans organizations to keep employers informed of veterans available for employment and veterans informed of opportunities for employment, and assist in every possible way in improving work conditions and advancing the employment of veterans.

Responsibility for developing policies and procedures governing the national farm placement program, and for directing and coordinating the activities of that program, is carried out through the Office of Farm Labor Service. The basic functions are to maintain a service for agricultural workers and employers which will provide adequate placement facilities for meeting year-round and seasonal labor requirements of agriculture and to place individual workers seeking employment in agriculture and to provide for the orderly and expeditious seasonal movement of migrant workers to successive jobs by providing placement service and current and reliable information regarding crop conditions and employment opportunities. The 

Office of Farm Labor Service also has responsibility for insuring that in the interstate recruitment of farm workers applicable standards are met relating to housing, transportation, and wages.

The Bureau also administers responsibilities under the act of July 12, 1951 (65 Stat. 119; 7 U.S.C. 1461 et seq.), dealing with the importation of agricultural workers from the Republic of Mexico. In addition, supplementary workers are brought in from

The Bureau's unemployment insurance program responsibilities include review and analysis of State laws and constructions thereof to determine if they are in conformity with the Social 

Security Act and the Federal Unem ployment Tax Act; review of State administration of unemployment insurance to determine whether the program is in compliance with the provisions of State law necessary to meet the 

Federal requirements, and whether individuals are denied benefits to which they are entitled under the State law and under the various agreements with the Secretary of Labor to carry out the

Federal Unemployment Compensation programs; establishment of feasible criteria for measuring administrative costs for use in determining the amounts of money necessary for proper adapting improved administrative procedures developed by the Bureau and efficient administration of the 

State unemployment compensation

laws; and furnishing assistance to the States on administrative and operating problems, in applying or adapting improved administrative procedures developed by the Bureau or by individual States, and in developing legislative recommendations designed to improve the program under the economy of each State. The 

Bureau also analyzes past trends and forecasts future trends in coverage, contributions, benefit rights, and benefit payments State by State and in the Nation as a whole; studies and recommends methods of improving the unemployment insurance program; disseminates information on the operation of the unemployment insurance program; assists the States in conducting studies of the effect of proposed program changes as well as their current programs, and in preparing evaluations of the solvency of the 

States' unemployment insurance benefit funds, as well as of the continued adequacy of the States' reserves and tax structures in light of actual or proposed amendments to the laws and the expected future incidence of unemployment; studies and develops policy recommendations concerning other governmental or private incomemaintenance programs which may affect the unemployment insurance system; directs the administration of a 

Federal program to pay allowances to workers who are undergoing approved training; and develops plans for the emergency payment of unemployment allowances in situations of enemy attack or national disaster. The Bureau's responsibilities for ex-servicemen's compensation under title XV of the Social Security Act include the mainte nance of central controls on all claimants and the review of State operations to insure that the title is properly administered. The Bureau's responsibilities for Federal employees' unemployment compensation, under title XV of the Social Security Act, include the de velopment and maintenance of procedures to be followed by Federal agencies in providing wage and separation information to State agencies, the assistance to State agencies in State operations, and the review of necessary 

Federal and State procedures to insure that the program is administered in accordance with title XV. 

The Federal Advisory Council on 

Employment Security, composed of representatives of employers, employees, and the public, was established by the Wagner-Peyser Act "to discuss problems and develop policy recommendations relating to employment and unemployment, and to insure impartiality, neutrality, and freedom from political influence in the solution of such problems." Under

Reorganization Plan 2 of 1949 the 

Council advises the Secretary of Labor and the Director of the Bureau with respect to the administration and coordination of the functions of the Bureau. 

Assistant Secretary for Labor-Management Relations 

The Assistant Secretary for Labor Management Relations has responsibility for the Department's labor-management relations activities, including those assigned to the Secretary by Executive order establishing policies governing employee-management cooperation in the Federal service.

Office of Welfare and Pension Plans 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 29, Chapter XI] 

This office was created by Secretary's Order 13-62 on April 24, 1962, for the purpose of administering and

enforcing those provisions of the Wel fare and Pension Plans Disclosure Act 

(72 Stat. 997, as amended; 29 U.S.C. 

301 note), for which the Secretary of

Labor has authority and responsibility. 

The act grants to the Secretary of 

Labor authority to issue rules and regu- lations governing the reporting and disclosure of information concerning the operation of welfare and pension plans and the bonding of persons handling the funds of such plans, specific power to investigate complaints and to secure compliance and restrain violations of the law through civil judicial proceedings, and power to issue binding and authoritative opinions and interpretations relating to the law. 

The Office, under the direction of a Director who is appointed by the Secretary of Labor, performs the following major functions: develops, receives, analyzes, and makes available for public disclosure reports submitted pursuant to the act; provides technical assistance and advice to persons and groups concerned with the reporting requirements of the act; recommends rules and regulations and communicates interpretations necessary to implement the act; and directs investigations under the provisions of the act.

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 29, Chapter IV]

Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act of 1959 (73 Stat. 519; 

29 U.S.C. 401 note) for which the 

Secretary of Labor has authority and responsibility.

Field offices of the Bureau provide information and assistance to persons seeking rights under the statutes, employers having the obligation to reemploy, and labor organizations concerned with the reemployment process. Aid is also given in local communities by reemployment rights advisers who serve on a voluntary basis under supervision of the field offices. 

Local offices of the State Employment 

Services (affiliated with the Bureau of 

Employment Security), local boards of the Selective Service System, contact offices of the Veterans' Administration, and service officers of veterans organizations serve as points of information and referral for those seeking advice with respect to reemployment rights.

Information and referral services are also provided at separation centers of the armed forces. 

Where a settlement cannot be reached through the machinery maintained by the Bureau, its cooperating agencies, and its local volunteers, the case may be referred to the Department of Justice for litigation if the ex-serviceman so requests. He is entitled to be represented by the United 

States attorney in court action if the latter deems his case to be meritorious. 

Wage and Hour and Public

Contracts Divisions 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 29, Chapter V; Title 41, Chapter 50] The Wage and Hour Division was established pursuant to the provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 

June 25, 1938 (52 Stat. 1060; 29

U.S.C. 201-219). The Public Con tracts Division was created to administer the Walsh-Healey Act of June 30, 1936 (49 Stat. 2036; 41 U.S.C. 3545). The two Divisions were consolidated by order of the Secretary of

Labor on August 21, 1942. The Wage 

and Hour and Public Contracts Divi sions are headed by an Administrator, appointed by the President with the consent of the Senate.

The Fair Labor Standards Act of 

1938, as amended, establishes, subject to specified exemptions, minimum wage, overtime compensation, and child labor standards for employees who, on an individual basis, are engaged in interstate or foreign commerce, including any closely related process or occupation directly essential thereto. The act also applies to any employee in an enterprise engaged in commerce or the production of goods for commerce, as defined in the law, including employees handling, selling, or otherwise working on goods that have been moved in or produced for commerce by any person. The

Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act re quires Federal Government supply contracts in amounts exceeding $10,000 to contain stipulations with respect to payment of minimum wages and overtime, nonemployment of child and convict labor, and observance of certain safety and health standards. The functions of the headquarters organization, or national office, are to develop nationwide policies and programs for the administration of the acts, to issue regulations and interpretations, to conduct economic research, to devise certification standards for learners, apprentices, full-time students, and handicapped workers, and to establish prevailing minimum wage rates under the Public Contracts Act. 

The Divisions operate on a decentralized basis through the geographical division of the country into 11 enforcement regions. Each region is headed by a regional director who is responsible to the Administrator for investigation and enforcement activities in his area. Field offices and field stations operate within each region under the supervision of the regional office. An area office is located in

Puerto Rico, and a formal reimbursa-

Wage and Hour and Public Contracts 

Divisions investigate and gather data regarding the wages, hours, and other conditions and practices of employment. They may investigate whatever facts, conditions, practices, or matters are considered necessary to find out whether any person has violated any provisions of the act or which may aid in enforcement of the act. The national office coordinates this enforcement program, directing a continuous evaluation of field activities to assure uniform and proper application of the acts. 

To recover unpaid minimum and/ or overtime wages, the Administrator may supervise payment of back wages and, in certain circumstances, the 

Secretary of Labor may bring suit for back pay upon the written request of the employee. The Secretary of Labor may also obtain a court injunction to restrain an employer from violating the law, including the unlawful withholding of proper minimum wage and overtime compensation.

The Divisions conduct wage determination activities under the acts encompassing: (1) the Public Con tracts wage determination program;

(2) the Fair Labor Standards Act industry committee program applicable to Puerto Rico, the Virgin 

Islands, and American Samoa; and (3) the special minimum wage programs authorized for learners, apprentices, full-time students, and handicapped workers. 

Regulations and research activities encompass programs for preparing interpretations and rulings on the general provisions of the acts and on exemption problems, directing economic research on administrative and legislative matters, conducting studies on the economic effect of minimum wage and overtime provisions, and

preparing and analyzing statistics of operations.

In response to a continual flow of inquiries from the general public and interested parties, the Divisions disseminate information and provide guidance concerning the functions and practices of the Divisions and the responsibilities and rights of employers and employees under both acts. 

Assistant Secretary for International Affairs 

The Assistant Secretary for International Affairs has responsibility for the Department's international activities. He supervises the Bureau of International Labor Affairs. He serves as the U.S. Government member of the Governing Body of the Interna tional Labor Organization (ILO), as head of the U.S. delegation to the Annual Conference of the ILO, and as a member of the Board of Foreign Service.

Bureau of International Labor Affairs 

The Bureau was established on December 31, 1959, replacing the Office of International Labor Affairs origi nally established in 1947. Under the policy direction of the Assistant Secretary of Labor for International Affairs, the Bureau is headed by an Administrator who is responsible for discharging Department of Labor functions in the international labor field. Under the policy direction of the Assistant Secretary, the Administrator is also charged with mobilizing, directing, and coordinating all other international activities of the Department's various specialized offices and bureaus. 

These functions and responsibilities of the Bureau include advising on the implications of international labor developments in relation to U.S. foreign and domestic policy, analyzing the impact of domestic policy and developments on labor aspects of foreign affairs, recommending operations designed to promote the United States national interest in the foreign labor field generally and with respect to specific areas of the world, and, with the assistance of other offices and bureaus, operating programs affecting labor which are designed to implement foreign policy.

The Bureau's staff of geographic area specialists develops detailed action programs in the field of labor for the various foreign countries. Through these country programs, the Government's efforts are coordinated to achieve U.S. foreign policy objectives as they relate to labor abroad. 

The Department of Labor has primary responsibility, under the overall foreign policy guidance of the Department of State, for United States participation in the International Labor 

Organization. 

The Bureau also carries out the Department's responsibilities for assisting the Department of State in the mancluding the labor attaché and Foreign agement of the Foreign Service, in Service labor-reporting programs (the 

Department has statutory membership for representation on delegations and on the Board of the Foreign Service); formulation of labor policy in connecin the United Nations Economic and tion with United States participation Social Council and its various commissions; for participation in the 

Trade Staff Committee and other interagency trade expansion activities and for staff support for the Depart ment's representatives on the Trade 

Expansion Act Advisory Committee and the Trade Executive Committee; and for participation of labor missions in the Government's international trade fair program. In these activities the Bureau relies upon technical as-

DE sistance from other bureaus of the Department. 

The Bureau coordinates and directs programs, both its own and those of other bureaus, which are carried on by the Department under various acts of 

Congress and under administrative agreements with other agencies for development of a fund of labor and manpower knowledge for use both in domestic and overseas programs; for development of a reservoir of labor and manpower experts; and for programs of technical cooperation and exchange of persons. As requested, consultants are supplied for foreign assignments, technical materials are furnished for use abroad, and training programs are conducted in the United States for foreign nationals. These programs are implemented in cooperation with the Department's bureaus and regional offices, State departments of labor, American trade unions, management, and other private organizations. 

The Bureau's responsibility for advice on the implications of international labor developments in relation to United States foreign and domestic policy calls for a continuing program of analysis of such labor developments and their economic and social implications in foreign countries. This program, as well as the other international programs of the Department, call for active and current research on foreign labor developments. In this connecthe tion, great reliance is placed upon 

Division of Foreign Labor Conditions of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which is responsible for research on labor around the world.

Women's Bureau 

The Women's Bureau, first estab lished as the Woman-In-Industry Serv ice in 1918, and made permanent by act approved June 5, 1920 (41 Stat. 

987; 29 U.S.C. 11), is charged with formulating standards and policies for promoting the welfare of wage-earning women, improving their working conditions, increasing their efficiency, and advancing their opportunities for profitable employment. It investigates and publishes reports upon matters pertaining to the welfare of working women. 

With the increasing importance of women in the labor force, the Director of the Women's Bureau now serves also as  of

Labor to provide a means of coordinating the activities of the Department of Labor and all its bureaus for the wider implementation of programs affecting all workers.

The Bureau is concerned with all women at work, or seeking work, and with their training and skills; with women in all fields of employment; with the student selecting her career; with the girl on her first job and the older woman worker; and with women who are both homemakers and wage earners.

Continuous research is carried on by the Bureau's technical experts to help it formulate policies and programs.

Bureau of Labor Standards 

The Bureau, established by departmental order in 1934, is a service agency to State labor departments and officials, and to labor, employer, and civic groups interested in improving working conditions. The Bureau promotes industrial safety and health, develops standards in the field of labor legislation and labor law administration, and in cooperation with the Bureau of International Labor Affairs assists in implementing international labor standards. In cooperation with the Bureau of International Labor

Affairs, it also carries on programs for

international exchange of persons and training. 

LEGISLATIVE AND ADMINISTRATIVE STANDARDS.-The Bureau provides technical information and assistance to groups and individuals interested in securing adequate and well administered labor laws. Basic materials are prepared, including summaries of various types of laws and information on the effective administration of labor laws covering a broad field of labor standards. Staff members give technical assistance to State labor departments, management, labor organizations, and civic groups on labor legislation and administration, and in adapting recommended standards and procedures to meet State needs. Governments, international agencies, and interested groups of other countries are provided information on labor law and its administration in this country. 

FEDERAL-STATE COORDINATION.- 

Through agreements negotiated by the 

Bureau between Federal and State agencies, the enforcement of wage, hour, industrial home work, child labor, and safety and health laws are coordinated to reduce duplication of inspection and to provide for the most effective use of Federal and State staffs.
