Bureau of Employees' Compensation 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 20, Chapter I] 

The Bureau, established in the Federal Security Agency under the provisions of Reorganization Plan 2, effective July 16, 1946, together with its functions was transferred to the Department of Labor pursuant to Reorganization Plan 19, effective May 24, 1950. 

The Bureau administers the following principal acts: 

1. The Federal Employees' Com pensation Act of September 7, 1916, which provides workmen's compensation benefits for civil officers and employees of the United States who suffer personal injuries while in the performance of duty, including persons who serve without compensation or for nominal compensation, or where acceptance or use of such services is authorized by an act of Congress, or provision is made by law for payment of the travel or other expenses of such person. 

2. The Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act of March 

4, 1927, which provides workmen's compensation benefits for employees in private enterprise while engaged in maritime employment on navigable waters of the United States. 

3. The District of Columbia Work men's Compensation Act of May 17, 1928, which extends the provisions of the Longshoremen's and Harbor

Workers' Compensation Act to pri vate employment in the District of Columbia. 

4. The Defense Bases Act of August 

16, 1941, which extends, with certain modifications, the provisions of the 

Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' 

Compensation Act to any employment (a) at U.S. military bases in foreign countries, (b) on lands occupied or used by the United States for military purposes outside the continental limits of the United States, (c) under a contract with the United States for the performance of any public work to be performed outside the continental United States, (d) under certain contracts approved and financed by the United States under the Mutual Security Act of 1954, as amended, (e) in the service of the American employers providing welfare or similar services for the benefit of the Armed 

Forces outside the continental United States. 

5. The War Hazards Compensation 

Act of December 2, 1942, which provides benefits for persons engaged in the employments listed under the Defense Bases Act who suffer injury or death as a result of a war risk hazard, and payments to dependents of employees missing from the place of employment due to the belligerent action of an enemy.

6. The act of July 26, 1946, pertain ing to the civilian war benefits program. 

7. Sections of the War Claims Act of 

July 3, 1948, providing benefits to civilian American citizens for injury, disability, or death caused by capture or detention by the Japanese Government at Midway, Guam, Wake Island, Philippine Islands, or other places subject to Federal jurisdiction, attacked or invaded by the Japanese. 

8. Provisions of the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act of August 7, 1953, extending the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation 

Act to operations conducted on the 

Outer Continental Shelf. 

9. The Nonappropriated Fund In strumentalities Act of July 18, 1958, extending the Longshoremen's and 

Harbor Workers' Act to employees of nonappropriated fund instrumentalities of the Armed Forces, such as Army and Air Force Exchange Service, Army and Air Force Motion Picture 

Service, Navy Ship's Stores Ashore,

Navy Exchanges, Coast Guard Ex changes. 

10. The Federal Employees' Com pensation Act which also extends to (a) employees of the District of Columbia Government, excluding the members of the police and fire departments, (b) members of the Coast 

Guard Reserve, (c) members of the 

Civil Air Patrol, and (d) members of the Reserve Officers Training Corps. 

The Bureau's director is appointed by the Secretary of Labor. The central office consists of three assistant directors, each of whom is aided by appropriate divisions. Nine district offices administer one or more of the various compensation acts. 

The Bureau is required to determine all questions arising under the Federal 

Employees' Compensation Act. (For provision for review of its decisions, see Employees' Compensation Appeals 

Board.) Among other functions, the 

Bureau is required to determine what 673525°-63- -22 employments come within the scope of the law, whether the injury for which compensation is claimed occurred while in the performance of duty, the period for which compensation may be paid, the amount thereof, and, in case of death, the persons entitled to receive such compensation. 

The Bureau is required to make arrangements to provide prompt and competent medical and hospital services for employees injured in the Federal service, and payment of monetary benefits. 

Under the Longshoremen's and 

Harbor Workers' Compensation Act, the Bureau authorizes insurance carriers to write insurance to secure the payment of compensation, authorizes employers to act as self-insurers, prepares opinions on questions of law for the guidance of deputy commissioners until such questions are finally settled by judicial determination, and supervises the defense of litigation arising out of this law. Decisions upon claims for compensation under this act, and local supervision of the enforcement of the act, are under deputy commissioners of the Bureau who have jurisdiction within the respective compensation districts to which they are assigned. The decision of the deputy commissioner in respect to a claim for compensation is subject to review by 

Federal district courts on questions of law. 

All compensation benefits authorized by this law are paid by the employer direct or through his authorized insurance carrier. The cost of administration of this law is paid from a 

Federal appropriation.

Employees' Compensation Appeals 

Board [For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 20, Chapter IV] 

Pursuant to authority contained in

Reorganization Plan 2, effective July

16, 1946, the Employees' Compensation Appeals Board was established in the Office of Special Services of the Federal Security Agency. Reorganiza tion Plan 19, effective May 24, 1950, provided for the transfer of the Board and its functions to the Department of 

Labor. The functions of the Federal 

Security Administrator with respect to the Board were transferred to the 

Secretary of Labor. 

The Board consists of three members appointed by the Secretary of Labor, one of whom is designated as chairman and administrative officer. It performs a quasi-judicial function in deciding appealed cases.

The Appeals Board was created for the purpose of reviewing and, subject to applicable law, making final decisions on appeals taken from determinations and awards with respect to employees of the Federal Government and of the District of Columbia in cases arising under the Federal 

Employees' Compensation Act of 

September 7, 1916, as amended (5 

U.S.C.A. 751-803). Appeals may be taken to the Board on disputed questions of law and fact and on the basis of abuse or failure to exercise discretion. 

An appeal may be filed pursuant to the Board's rules of procedure which may be found in title 20 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Part 501. Application for review forms may be obtained from the Board, but informal applications which set forth grounds of the appeal are also acceptable. 

The Board may review a case only on the record certified to it by the 

Bureau of Employees' Compensation; new evidence may not be submitted to the Board. The procedure in respect to appeals includes the holding, upon request, of hearings for the presentation of oral argument. The decisions of the Board are contained in orders affirming or modifying the action of the Bureau, or remanding cases for further development, as may be necessary. Cases decided upon the merits are accompanied by a written opinion. The decision of the Board in appealed cases is final. 

Assistant Secretary for Policy Planning and Research 

The Assistant Secretary for Policy

Planning and Research has responsibility for reviewing programs, developing program projections for future periods, and providing leadership and coordination of the Department's research programs. He supervises the

Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Consumer Program Adviser. 

Bureau of Labor Statistics 

The Bureau of Labor, the predeces sor of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, was established in the Department of the Interior, by act of June 27, 1884.

In 1913, after several changes in status, it became the Bureau of Labor Statistics in the newly created Department of Labor. The Bureau is the Govern ment's principal factfinding agency in the field of labor economics, partic ularly with respect to the collection and analysis of data on employment and manpower, productivity and technological developments, wages, industrial relations, work injuries, prices, and costs and standards of living. no 

The Bureau of Labor Statistics has enforcement or administrative functions. Practically all of the basic data it collects from workers, businessagencies are supplied by voluntary comen, and from other governmental operation based on their interest in and need for the analyses and summaries which result. The research and statistical projects planned by the Bureau grow out of the needs of these groups, as well as the needs of Congress and the Federal and State governments.

JAUMI 

The information collected is issued in special bulletins and in its official publication, the Monthly Labor Review.

EMPLOYMENT AND THE LABOR 

FORCE.-Data are published each month on the labor force, employment, and unemployment, by age, sex, occupation, etc., based on a sample survey of the population. At recurring intervals the surveys provide estimates of the educational attainment of the labor force, the employment of students, family relationship of workers, and other personal and economic characteristics of the labor force.

National estimates are published each month on the employment of wage and salary workers in 365 manufr facturing and nonmanufacturing industries. In cooperation with State agencies, comparable employment data are provided for all the States and for the more important metropolitan areas. 

Labor turnover rates are provided for 223 industries in manufacturing, mining, and communications. All the Government's current statistics on the labor force, employment, and unemployment are published monthly in 

Employment and Earnings. 20 

The Bureau conducts studies of trends in unemployment, of problems affecting particular groups in the working population, such as youth and older workers, and prepares analyses and projections of the changing size and composition of the labor force. In addition, the Bureau is responsible for assessment of the military manpower pool and for projections of potential manpower resources, in relation to requirements under conditions of national emergency.

EARNINGS, WAGES, AND HOURS.- 

Gross average hourly and weekly earnings, and average weekly hours, for production or nonsupervisory workers, are issued currently by the Bureau for about 323 industries on a national basis. Average weekly overtime hours are published currently for 143 manufacturing industry groups. Through the cooperative State program, similar data are made available for all States and the more important metropolitan areas. These statistics are reported monthly in Employment and Earnings.

Occupational wage surveys are made annually in 80 major labor markets. 

These studies provide information on the level and distribution of wages and salaries for office clerical, professional and technical, maintenance and power plant, and custodial, warehousing, and shipping occupational categories. 

Work schedules and supplementary wage benefits are also summarized in these studies. A more comprehensive national survey of salaries for professional, administrative, technical, and clerical occupations is made annually. 

Occupational wage surveys are made in selected industries covering major manufacturing and nonmanufacturing industries over a 5-year cycle. A few industries are studied annually; most industries, however, are studied at 3to 5-year intervals. Information ist provided on a national and regional basis and for selected areas of concentration. Work schedules and supplementary wage benefits are also summarized in these studies.

Distributions of production and related workers and of other nonsupervisory employees by straight-time average hourly earnings are periodically established in studies that provide national and regional estimates for manufacturing and selected nonmanufacturing industries. 

Annual surveys are made in 52 cities of wage rates agreed upon in union contracts for a limited number of occupations in printing and publishing, local streetcar and bus operations, the building trades, and motor trucking. 

Quarterly data are available for 100 cities for seven selected occupations in the construction trades. 

Information on current trends in wage rates and wage practices is presented in a monthly report summarizing current wage settlements.

In

addition, statistical summaries are prepared quarterly and annually. Chronologies showing the historical development of wage rate changes are presented for important bargaining situations in selected industries. A series of indexes of changes in wages and salarics for selected occupational groups are maintained. 

Studies of employer expenditures on selected fringe benefits and of the composition of payroll hours are made over a 3-year cycle in manufacturing and in selected nonmanufacturing industries. 

LABOR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS.- 

The Bureau maintains a file of current union contracts and constitutions which is used as factual background material by unions, employers, and conciliation agencies in the settlement of industrial disputes, and as a guide to the preparation of new agreements.

The Bureau publishes analyses of union agreements in individual industries and agreement provisions concerning such subjects as vacations, overtime, and grievance procedures. 

Similar studies of health, insurance, and pension plans, and other employee benefit plans and of the substantive provisions of union constitutions are also made. Current statistics on work stoppages resulting from industrial disputes are issued monthly with detailed analyses available annually. The Bureau publishes a biennial Directory of 

National and International Labor

Unions in the United States, and studies of union membership, structure, and procedures. 

PRODUCTIVITY.- 

-The Bureau publishes annual indexes of output per man-hour and unit man-hour requirements for the private economy and broad industrial groupings such as manufacturing, mining, and agriculture. Annual indexes are published comparing trends in productivity with those of employment costs per hour, employment costs per unit of output, and prices for the total private and nonagricultural sector of the economy. 

Indexes are also prepared for selected industries in manufacturing and nonmanufacturing relating output to the man-hours of production workers and of all employees. 

The Bureau conducts studies of technological developments and automation and their implications for productivity and manpower requirements. 

These studies deal with the adjustments made by plants introducing new kinds of equipment, including planning, training, and transfer of workers, the outlook for innovations and for technological developments in different industries, with the projected impact on productivity and changes in number and kind of workers who will be needed.

Studies of the importance of construction in generating employment include estimates for direct, on-site construction activities and for indirect, off-site activities such as manufacturing, mining, and transportation. They also provide information on the kind of construction labor used, the timing of construction, and the kinds of materials used.

INDUSTRIAL HAZARDS AND WORKING CONDITIONS.-The Bureau conducts quarterly surveys on work injuries in manufacturing, and annual surveys in both manufacturing and nonmanufac turing in a large number of industries. 

National estimates are prepared annually for all disabling work injuries, by extent of disability for major industry groups. Special studies are made in industries with high accident rates, to determine accident causes and thereby to stimulate accident prevention programs in the industries studied. 

Technical services are extended to

State agencies to assist them in the development of better accident statistics. Currently, State-Federal cooperative injury rate surveys are con ducted in 12 States.

OCCUPATIONAL OUTLOOK.-The Bu reau publishes reports on the longrange employment outlook in important occupations and industries.

Data on employment trends, earnings, hours, industrial hazards, collectivebargaining agreements, and technological trends collected by the Bureau are included for guidance purposes, together with information from other Government and private sources. 

Conclusions of these studies are published in the Occupational Outlook Handbook, a new edition of which will be published late in 1963, and The 

Occupational Outlook Quarterly, a periodical published four times in the school year.

LABOR CONDITIONS IN OTHER COUN- 

TRIES.-Basic information and current developments in the labor field in other countries are covered in the Bureau's program. Discussions of the general labor situation in individual countries and summaries of available information on a particular subject in the field of labor economics throughout the world appear in the Monthly Labor

Review and in special reports published from time to time in foreign labor reports and bulletins. The Bureau also issues a monthly summary called Labor Developments Abroad.

International comparisons of labor statistics in general and unit labor costs and labor force statistics, in particular are also studied and reported on. 

In cooperation with the Bureau of 

International Labor Affairs, the Bureau of Labor Statistics provides op portunities for labor statisticians from other countries to study its methods and on request sends consultants to countries undertaking new statistical programs in the labor field.

A further description of the international work of the Bureau of Labor Statistics is found under Bureau of International Labor Affairs.

The Solicitor of Labor 

The Solicitor has responsibility for all the legal activities of the Department, for the coordination and preparation of the Department's legislative proposals, reports and testimony on proposed legislation, including executive branch clearances, and for the administration of the Davis-Bacon and related acts except as specifically reserved to the Secretary. He serves as legal adviser to the Secretary and other officials of the Department.

Office of the Solicitor The Solicitor is the chief law officer of the Department of Labor. In such capacity, with the assistance of the 

Deputy Solicitor, he exercises direction and supervision over the legal work of the entire Department. Responsible to him is an immediate staff of assistants and attorneys in Washington and in the field offices of the Department throughout the United States and Puerto Rico.

The Solicitor is also empowered to perform the duties of the Secretary of 

Labor in certain instances. Pursuant to delegation of authority from the Secretary, he exercises final authority in the 

Department over the withdrawal of originals and copies of files, records, and documents of the Department, in determining the necessity of publishing documents in the Federal Register, and over tort claims arising out of the Department's activities; performs administrative and interpretative functions under the Davis-Bacon Act and related prevailing-wage statutes, the 

Copeland Act, the Federal Eight-Hour

Laws, and the functions of the Department under Reorganization Plan 14 of 1950 and the statutes listed in the Department's Regulations, Part 5 (29 

CFR Part 5).

Among the major Department activities serviced by the Solicitor are those relating to manpower, minimum wages and maximum hours, child labor, employment security, the Mexican labor program, veterans readjustment assistance program, workmen's compensation, veterans' reemployment rights, apprenticeship training, safety of longshoremen, labor-management laws, welfare and pension plans reporting and disclosure, and international labor affairs.

The Solicitor's Office interprets statutes administered or coordinated in the Department and furnishes legal serv ices in connection with hearings and other administrative proceedings leading to formulation of rules and regula tions implementing such statutes.

The Solicitor is in charge of the liti gation of the Department. He represents the Secretary of Labor in the institution and prosecution of all civil court actions involving the Fair Labor 

Standards Act, including preparation of briefs and argument of appellate cases. His Office assists in the preparation, trial, and briefing of criminal cases under the Fair Labor Standards

Act, and civil actions to recover damages under the Public Contracts Act; represents the Department officials in administrative hearing; and performs legal services in the preparation, in-

The Administrative Assistant Secretary

The Administrative Assistant Sec retary has responsibility for the 

Department's budgetary and fiscal management, personnel management, administrative management, organization, the Library, and administrative services activities. He is assisted by the Deputy Administrative Assistant 

Secretary, who serves as the Department's Budget Officer and Comptroller.

• as fo 

.::.111 

Office of the Administrative Assistant 

Secretary

The Office directs and coordinates all matters of administration and management in the Department and handles or supervises all contacts with 

Congress on budget matters. 

It reviews, evaluates, and approves proposed and existing programs to assure compliance with Department policies, plans, and budgetary directives; determines amounts and adequacy of presentation of budget estimates and apportionments. The 

Office develops, reviews, and approves organization structures within the several bureaus, and promulgates departmental regulations and procedures governing all budget, fiscal management, management analysis, and office service functions. It develops and maintains all major relationships outside the Department on administration and management matters and coordinates contacts with the Bureau of the

Budget, except those involving substantive legislation.

The Office provides departmentwide services concerned with real property, space, communications, messenger service, central mail room facilities, parking space facilities, travel arrangements, local transportation facilities, procurement of articles and services, centralized duplicating and printing, and centralized stock and shipping It prepares budgets for the Office of the Secretary and certain bureaus and offices and provides centralized accounting and payroll rooms. services. 

The Office develops and coordinates all plans and procedures necessary to provide management, fiscal, and administrative services for the execution of the mobilization and civil defense responsibility of the Department, including communications, establishing and maintaining relocation sites, safeguarding records and providing physical security measures. 

The Office directs and coordinates the personnel program of the Department and is responsible for the standards, procedures, and methods under which the program operates. It also directs management programs to improve employee-management relations, employee morale, employee training and utilization, and employee work performance appraisal and improvement.

LIBRARY.-The Librarian operates under the direct supervision of the Administrative Assistant Secretary and is responsible for the effective organization and administration of the library services of the Department. The Li brarian approves all purchases of books, newspapers, periodicals, and other publications for the Department in Washington and in the field.

The Library is a specialized collection of about 413,000 books, periodicals, and pamphlets on labor and related subjects. It provides reference service to the staff of the Department and to the public, circulates books and periodicals to the staff, and lends material to other libraries.

Department of Health, Education, and

Welfare was created by Reorganization 

Plan 1 of 1953. Under provisions of the act approved April 1, 1953 (67 

Stat. 18; 5 U. S. C. 623), the Plan became effective on April 11, 1953. The

Plan abolished the Federal Security 

Agency, created by Reorganization Plan I of 1939, and transferred all functions of the Federal Security Ad ministrator to the Secretary of Health,

Education, and Welfare and all components of the Agency to the Department.

PURPOSE.-The Department was established for the purpose of improving the administration of those agencies of the Government the major responsibilities of which are to promote the general welfare in the fields of health, education, and social security.

ORGANIZATION.-The Department is administered under the supervision and direction of the Secretary. The structure of the Department is shown. in the organization chart which appears on page 602.

Health, Education, and Welfare, as the head of an executive department, reports directly to the President, supervises and directs the Department, and carries out Federal responsibilities in relation to three federally aided corporations: American Printing House for the Blind, Gallaudet College, and 

Howard University.

Printing House for the Blind, Gallaudet 

College, and Howard University.

OFFICE OF PUBLIC INFORMATION.- 

This Office is responsible for the general direction and supervision of all public information activities of the Department.

ASSISTANT SECRETARY (FOR LEGIS- LATION). The Assistant Secretary 

(for Legislation) serves as principal staff adviser to the Secretary in the coordination of the development and presentation of the Department's legislative program; serves as liaison with external committees, commissions, organizations, or agencies dealing with legislative matters; and directs the Of fice of Program Analysis. 

ASSISTANT SECRETARY.-The Assist ant Secretary serves as principal staff adviser to the Secretary on departmentwide international programs, congressional liaison, and water supply and pollution control; and through the respective staff offices, coordinates the activities of the Department in these fields.

SPECIAL ASSISTANT TO THE SECRE- TARY (HEALTH AND MEDICAL AF- 

FAIRS). The Special Assistant to the

Secretary (Health and Medical Af fairs) reviews the health and medical programs of the Department and advises the Secretary with respect to the improvement of such programs and with respect to necessary legislation in health and medical fields.

OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUN- SEL.-This Office renders legal advice and opinions on questions which arise in connection with administration and operation of programs and participates in the formulation of the Department's legislative program.

OFFICE OF FIELD ADMINISTRATION.- The Director of Field Administration serves as principal adviser to the Secretary in the coordination of the field activities of the Department. The

Office administers a program of fiscal audits of grant-in-aid funds, a program of assistance to the States in the administration of merit systems for personnel involved in grant-in-aid programs, and the statutory functions of the Secretary with respect to surplus property utilization. 

OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATION.-The 

Administrative Assistant Secretary serves as principal adviser to the Secretary on administration; coordinates management responsibilities with program policies and operations. The 

Office performs all of the functions of the Secretary in the field of administrative and financial management; provides departmentwide coordination, leadership, and guidance on budgetary and financial management, personnel management, organization, administrative management, and administrative services. Public Health Service 

Regulations, Title 42, Chapter I]  

Public Health Service has its origin in an act of July 16, 1798 (ch. 77, 1 Stat. 

605), authorizing marine hospitals for the care of American merchant seamen. Subsequent legislation has vastly broadened the scope of its activities. 

The Public Health Service Act of 

July 1, 1944 (58 Stat. 682; 42 U. S. C. 

201), consolidated and revised substantially all existing legislation relating to the Public Health Service, including title VI of the Social Secu rity Act, and provided for greater assistance to States, for coordinated research, for establishment of a national tuberculosis control program, and for expansion of the commissioned corps. The basic Public Health Serv ice statute has been amended by numerous acts, all of which place additional responsibilities on the Service. 

The International Health Research 

Act of 1960 (74 Stat. 365; 42 U.S.C. 

242f) authorizes the Public Health 

Service to make grants to United

States universities to establish international centers for medical research in cooperation with foreign medical institutions. 

PURPOSE.-The Public Health Serv ice, under the direction of the Surgeon 

General, is the Federal agency specifically charged with responsibilities for protecting and improving the health of the people of the Nation. It is also responsible for collaborating with governments of other countries and with international organizations in world health activities. The major functions of the Service are: (1) to conduct and support research and training in the medical and related sciences, and in public health methods and administration; (2) to provide medical and hospital services to persons authorized to receive care from the Service, to aid in the development of the Nation's hospital and related facilities, and to prevent the introduction of communicable diseases into the United States and its possessions; and (3) to assist the 

States and other governments in the application of new knowledge for the prevention and control of disease, the maintenance of a healthful environment, and the development of community health services.

ORGANIZATION.-The activities of the Service are organized into four bureaus: Office of the Surgeon Gen eral, Bureau of Medical Services, Bureau of State Services, and National 

Institutes of Health; and the National

Library of Medicine. The Congress has authorized the following National advisory councils to assist the Surgeon General in carrying out specific func tions: National Advisory Health Coun- Health Research Facilities, National cil, National Advisory Council on

Also, Congress requires the Surgeon General to hold annual conferences with three groups-State and Territorial health officers, representatives of State agencies concerned with mental health, and representatives of State agencies concerned with hospital and medical facilities survey and construction. 

In order to maintain direct contact with State and local authorities, with field offices of other Federal agencies, and with other official and nonofficial organizations concerned with its activities, the Service maintains a staff in the regional offices of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare.

These staffs are headed by regional health directors who represent the Surgeon General in interpreting and carrying out the broad policies of the 

Service. The regional health director is assisted by two associate regional health directors, one representing the programs of community health and the other, the programs of environmental health. The regional staffs work with 

State authorities in developing and maintaining plans, programs, and budgets for Federal-State cooperative health programs. 

Office of the Surgeon General

The Office of the Surgeon General is a bureau composed mainly of staff services for the three operating bureaus and for the Surgeon General in his overall management of the organization. Its various divisions and offices assist in (1) studying the health needs of the Nation; (2) providing overall program and policy direction to Service activities in the international health field and in the planning, negotiation, and administration of Service responsibilities for international health serv ices with Federal agencies and international organizations; (3) directing and coordinating the Service's information, publications, and public inquiries programs; (4) developing general plans and programs under which personnel administration will be carried on within the Service; (5) managing budget and fiscal activities; (6) providing for the management of all areas of general services; (7) facilitating organizational and procedural improvements and the general management of the Service; (8) supervising Public 

Health Service regional organizations and coordinating Public Health Service Federal-State activities; (9) preparing the Nation to meet the health and water needs of the civilian population in the event of a national disaster; and (10) operating the National Center for Health Statistics which is the principal statistical arm of the Public 

Health Service and one of the major general-purpose statistical organizations of the Federal Government. 

Through its National Health Survey 

Division, the Center conducts surveys and special studies of the population of the United States to determine the extent of morbidity and disability and to gather information related to these events. Areas of interest include the amounts and type and services received, the economic and social impact of morbidity and disability, and methods of financing family health care.

Bureau of Medical Services

The Bureau of Medical Services is the medical arm of the Public Health 

Service primarily concerned with developing and directing certain medical care and health services programs, and preventing the introduction of disease and the entry of mentally and physically defective aliens into the United

States. 

Medical care is provided eligible beneficiaries through a system of Public Health Service hospitals, outpatient clinics, and offices located throughout the United States where seamen employed on vessels of U.S. Registry, Coast Guard and other uniformed services personnel, and other legal beneficiaries receive hospitalization, medical and dental care, and preventive health services. In addition, dependents of uniformed services personnel are entitled to medical care and emergency dental care at such hospitals and outpatient clinics, A pro gram of therapeutic and preventive health services is provided for Indians and Alaska natives of the United States through area and field offices operating PHS Indian and Alaska native hospitals, health centers, school health centers, practical nurse training schools, and health stations; hand through contracts with local governmental and nongovernmental resources. By direction of the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, administrative supervision is provided Freedmen's Hospital in the District of 

Columbia. This is a general hospital for the treatment of acute medical and surgical conditions, with an extensive system of specialized clinics for out- 31 patients. The hospital provides internship and clinical experience for medical students and graduates of Howard University. [For regulations codified under Freedmen's Hospital, see Code of Federal Regula tions, Title 42, Chapter IV] 

Public laws and regulations to prevent the introduction of quarantinable and other dangerous communicable diseases into the United States are implemented through a system of worldwide epidemiological vigilance and inspection of arriving persons, animals, and things at ports and airports involved in international traffic. The medical provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act to exclude persons who present a danger to public health or a probability of an economic burden to public funds are implemented by medical examinations of aliens performed abroad, and by medical inspections at ports of arrival. 

Technical advice and personnel are furnished to assist other Federal agencies in health care programs for their employees and beneficiaries. Professional supervision and consultation are provided Service personnel directing medical care programs and/or performing medical services for certain other Federal agencies. The Bureau of State Services is the principal operating bureau of the Service for Federal-State and interstate health programs. It gives general direction to activities in the two broad areas of Community Health and Environ mental Health designed to aid the

States and communities in developing, establishing, and maintaining effective

programs for the prevention, treatment, and control of diseases and for the prevention or control of environmental health hazards.

Within these areas, the Bureau conducts research; provides training, furnishes consultation and technical assistance to States and localities; conducts field surveys, investigations, and demonstrations; provides emergency disaster and epidemic aid to States; enforces corrective measures under certain statutes; conducts public information and education programs; administers various grant programs. 

COMMUNITY HEALTH.-Bureau pro grams in this area are concerned with: (1) the development of techniques for the application of scientific observations in the fields of biology and medicine; (2) the social and behavioral aspects of major health problems; (3) the organization and delivery of comprehensive community health services; (4) the development and effective utilization of professional, technical, and supplementary manpower; and (5) the planning, construction, coordination, and operation of hospital, medical, and related facilities appropriate to the needs of communities. 

These programs include the control of chronic diseases such as heart disease, cancer, diabetes, and arthritis; the control of communicable diseases (including tuberculosis and venereal diseases); the conservation of sight, hearing, and speech and the control of neurological disorders; the development and coordination of community health programs to remedy and alleviate problems of the aged; the provision of consultation on nursing home and noninstitutional care services; the administration of health programs in the fields of nursing services and resources, dental services and resources, and accident prevention; and the administration of a construction program for health facilities (Hill-Burton Act).

ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH.-Bureau programs in this area are concerned with: (1) the conduct and support of national programs to determine the nature, methods for effective measurement, and the health effects of environmental contaminants, including the total or cumulative effect as well as the individual effects on man; (2) the development of techniques and methods for practical control programs and for the maintenance of a healthful environment; (3) the study of political, social, and economic factors related to urbanization and metropolitan complexes as they affect environmental health, in order to develop effective methods of organization and administration in this field; (4) the development and effective utilization of professional and technical manpower and other resources for the broad field of environmental health; and (5) the administration of interstate quarantine regulations and water pollution control enforcement measures. These programs include air pollution control; water supply and water pollution control; milk, food, shellfish, interstate and community sanitation; occupational health, radiological health, and arctic health; with research centers at 

Cincinnati, Ohio, and Anchorage,

Alaska, as well as specialized operational activities at numerous field stations located throughout the country. 

National Institutes of Health The National Institutes of Health, the principal research arm of the Public Health Service, is primarily concerned with the extension of basic knowledge regarding the health problems of man and how to cope with them.

Fundamental laboratory and clini cal research in causes, prevention, and methods of diagnosis and treatment of cancer, cardiovascular and geriatric diseases, allergy and infectious diseases, arthritis and metabolic diseases, -11 Nord 101 Mikill 11

National Library of Medicine The National Library of Medicine comprises the greatest collection of medical literature in the world, exceeding a million pieces. The Library acquires and pre serves books, periodicals, and other library materials; organizes these materials by appropriate cataloging and indexing; publishes bibliographical guides to medical literature; and provides reference and research assistance.

PURPOSE.-The Office of Education is the principal agency of the Federal Government responsible for formulating educational policy and coordinating educational activities at the national level. In carrying out its programs it cooperates with other Government agencies, the States and Territories, professional groups and institutions, citizen groups and individuals, and international agencies. 

Its major functions are: (1) to collect and disseminate information with respect to education in the States and in other countries; (2) to make studies and provide services of a national character; (3) to evaluate educational and social trends affecting education; (4) to identify some of the larger problems in education calling for immediate research and action programs; (5) to provide major leadership and impetus for educational research; (6) to provide professional educational advisory service primarily based on findings of research and to aid in improving educational practice; and (7) to administer grants-in-aid to education.

Social Security  Social Security Administration, under a Commissioner for Social Security, was established by the Federal Security Administrator pursuant to Reorgan ization Plan II, effective July 16, 1946, which abolished the Social Security Board (see appendix A) and transferred its functions, along with functions of the Children's Bureau, to the 

Federal Security Administrator. Dele gated to the Commissioner for Social Security were functions in connection with old-age and survivors insurance, unemployment insurance, and public assistance, and most maternal and child welfare programs. Other duties have subsequently been delegated to or transferred from the Administration by law or Presidential order.

The position of Commissioner for Social Security was reestablished as 

Commissioner of Social Security in the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare by Reorganization Plan 1, effective April 11, 1953. The Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare on 

January 28, 1963, reorganized the 

Social Security Administration, estab lishing the old-age, survivors and disability insurance (OASDI) and Federal credit union programs as the pri mary missions of the Administration. 

The Bureau of Old-Age and Survivors 

Insurance was abolished as a bureau and the Bureau of Family Services and the Children's Bureau were transferred to a new Welfare Administration. 

PURPOSE. The Social Security Ad ministration administers the Federal old-age, survivors and disability insur ance programs (title II of the Social qualifications of secondary school guidance and counseling personnel; and contracts for the operation of modern foreign language institutes and centers and for the conduct of research in foreign language teaching and learning. Administration Security Act, as amended, and title VII and XI of that act as they pertain to the Social Security Administration), and the Federal credit union program 

(Federal Credit Union Act). It is responsible for studying problems of poverty and insecurity and the contributions that can be made to their solution by social insurance and related programs and for making recommendations for the most effective methods of improving social and economic security through social insurance. 

The purpose of old-age, survivors and disability insurance (OASDI) is to provide continuing income for individuals and their families as partial replacement of earnings lost through old-age or disability retirement or death. The OASDI program provides for the coverage of almost all persons engaged in gainful employment, including the military, the major exceptions being Federal civilian employees under a retirement system; selfemployed doctors of medicine; and domestics, agricultural workers, and selfemployed persons having very low earnings. Entitlement to benefits is determined from the insured status of the individual; the age and relationship of the individual and his dependents; the application for such benefits; and in the case of disability benefits, the extent and expected duration of disability. Benefits are payable monthly in amounts related to the average monthly earnings of the insured person. A lump sum death benefit is payable under certain conditions.

The Federal credit union program promotes thrift by encouraging coop-

erative, systematic saving and by mak- 

King credit available in the short-term, small loan field at reasonable rates of interest, for credit union members. To accomplish these purposes, Federal e te credit unions provide convenient facilities for encouraging the development of habits of consistent regular saving out of current earnings.
